title: Northern Lights, Snow Monkeys & a Moose Who Can Fly
note_intro: There are 195 countries on Earth, and Mossy the moose would like to take you and your child to every last one. Each adventure is written to spark wonder, share a laugh, and usher you both to the edge of dreamland. One night you’ll stand where the ground breathes steam; the next, on the banks of a river as wide as the sea. Every night, Mossy pulls on his leather flying helmet, grows as big as a pony, and carries your child to a new corner of the world. This book holds the first 28 nights of that journey. Your child is always the explorer. You get to ride along.
author: Daly Henrikson writes bedtime stories for children who ask “where does the sun go?” right before falling asleep, and for the grown-ups who still don’t quite know how to answer. He believes a good bedtime story should do two things at once: settle a restless mind and quietly widen it, one country, one custom, one small wonder at a time.

Bedtime Passport began as a nightly ritual with his own sons, a way to turn the wait for sleep into a small trip somewhere new. Night by night, it grew into a journey around the whole globe, told in the soft, unhurried voice of someone tucking a child in.

Daly believes the world is too big, too strange and too beautiful to save for someday. He also believes every story is better read aloud by someone who loves you. That is the one part he can’t do for you.
series: Keep your goggles on for more books in the Bedtime Passport series!
The first two books are out now, and five more are planned for the coming months: 196 nights in all, one for every country on Earth, plus a journey back home.
There is even a rumor that Mossy is working on an eighth book of special places that aren’t on the usual list of the world’s countries.
Learn more about the series and sign up for updates at www.bedtimepassport.com.

weeks.region: The Arctic Rim & Land of the Midnight Sun

nights.title: The Land Where the Ground Breathes
nights.pronunciations: Althing [AHL-thing], one of the world’s oldest parliaments; Thingvellir [THING-vet-lir], where it met; tölt [TURLT], the Icelandic horse’s smooth fifth gait; Jólabókaflóð [YOH-la-boh-ka-floth], the Christmas Book Flood; Góða nótt [GOH-tha NOHT], good night.
nights.anchor: 874 AD (first permanent Norse settlement by Ingólfur Arnarson) and 930 AD (the first Althing).
facts: An Old, Old Parliament:
In 930 AD, Icelandic families gathered at Thingvellir to make laws together. Their Althing still meets today, and it is one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
Power from the Earth:
Hot water from deep underground warms about nine out of ten Icelandic homes, and nearly all of the country’s electricity comes from hot earth and rushing rivers.
Pure Viking Horses:
Icelandic horses came with the Vikings over 1,000 years ago, and no other horses have been allowed in since. They can do a super-smooth fifth gait called the tölt.
Brand-New Mosquitoes (and No Moose):

For as long as anyone knew, Iceland was one of the only places on Earth with no mosquitoes. Then, in October 2025, a few were found there for the very first time, and scientists are now watching to see if they stay. Iceland has no wild moose, either.
The Christmas Book Flood:
On Christmas Eve, Icelanders give each other books, then read in bed while eating chocolate.
story: There is a moose at the end of your bed.

He is your moose. Soft and brown, about the size of a pillow, with big, kind eyes. But tonight he is wearing something new: an old leather flying helmet, with two holes cut in the top for his antlers, a pair of round goggles pushed up on his forehead, and a white pilot’s scarf around his neck. Under one hoof, he holds a small blue book.

“Evening, explorer!” says the moose, in a deep, rumbly voice. “I’m Mossy. Captain Mossy, if you like. This is your Bedtime Passport. It only works when you’re sleepy. And every night, it will fly us somewhere amazing.”
“Fly?” you whisper. “But moose can’t fly.”

Mossy peeks at you over his goggles. “Moose,” he says, “can do all sorts of things when nobody is watching. When I say the magic words, pull your goggles down. Like this.” He holds two hoof-circles over his eyes. “Ready? Goggles on!”

You make circles with your fingers and hold them over your eyes. The Passport flashes blue. And Mossy grows. And grows. And GROWS, until he is as big as a pony, and you are sitting on his warm, wide back, holding his antlers like handlebars.
WHOOOOSH! Your bedroom folds up like a paper map, and you are flying.
When his hooves touch down, the ground is warm.

Warm! You slide off, and the black rock under your toes feels as toasty as a sleeping cat. All around, white steam curls up out of cracks in the ground. Fffssshhh. Fffssshhh. It looks as if the whole world is breathing out.

“Welcome to Iceland,” says Mossy, pushing up his goggles. “Long ago, a Viking sailed here in a wooden ship. He saw all this steam and thought it was smoke! So he named the place Reykjavik [RAY-kya-veek]. It means ‘Smoky Bay.’”
“Was it smoke?” you ask.
“Nope!” Mossy chuckles, a rumbly chuckle you can feel in your tummy. “It’s heat from deep inside the Earth. Iceland is full of volcanoes and geysers that go... oh dear. Stand back!”

KER-SPLOOOOSH! A fountain of hot water shoots up taller than a house. Mossy tries to hide behind a rock. The rock is much smaller than Mossy. His whole bottom sticks out, and the water rains down on it. You laugh until you snort.

“Here’s the clever part,” says Mossy, wiping his goggles. “Icelanders use all that heat. Pipes carry hot water from underground to warm houses and even outdoor swimming pools. You can swim outside in the snow, snug as a bath!”
Something shaggy trots out of the mist. It is a small, sturdy horse with a mane like a tangled curtain. She stops. She stares at Mossy.
“She’s never seen a moose before,” Mossy whispers. “There are no moose in Iceland. Well. There is one now.”
The horse sniffs Mossy’s nose. Mossy sniffs back. Friends!

You climb onto the horse, and she sets off, so smooth you hardly bounce at all. “Icelandic horses have a special way of walking called the tölt [TURLT],” says Mossy, flying low beside you. “It’s so smooth you could carry a cup of cocoa and not spill a drop. Their great-great-great-grandparents came here with the Vikings, more than a thousand years ago.”

The horse carries you to a wide, grassy valley between tall rock walls. It is called Thingvellir [THING-vet-lir]. “Long ago, families met here every summer to make rules together,” Mossy says softly. “They called it the Althing [AHL-thing]. It still meets today. It’s one of the oldest parliaments in the world. A parliament is a group of people who make a country’s rules.”
Then Mossy tilts one big ear. Then the other. “Listen. Do you hear anything missing?”
You listen. Wind. Water. The horse breathing. Hardly any buzzing at all.

“For a very long time, Iceland had no mosquitoes,” says Mossy. “Not one! Then, not long ago, someone spotted a few, for the very first time.” He wiggles his nose. “Back home, mosquitoes tickle my nose all summer. I hope these ones stay very small.”
The sky turns the color of blueberries. You come to a tiny house with a roof made of real grass. Mossy squeezes through the door, antlers first. Inside, books fill the shelves from floor to ceiling.
“On Christmas Eve,” Mossy says, and his voice is slow and yawny now, “Icelanders give each other books. Then they read in bed and eat chocolate. It’s called the Christmas Book Flood.”
“That sounds like the best night ever,” you murmur.
“It’s a tie with tonight,” says Mossy.

You snuggle under a heavy wool blanket. Through the window, green ribbons of light swish slowly across the sky, like a scarf made of stars. The Northern Lights. Under the house, the warm ground hums. The horse is asleep in her field. Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, curls up at the end of your bed, and pulls his goggles down over his sleepy eyes.
“Whisper it with me,” he says. “Góða nótt [GOH-tha NOHT].”
“Góða nótt,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and lie very still under the Northern Lights. Watch the green ribbons swish across the sky, slower and slower, softer and softer, while the warm ground hums beneath you.
nights.alt: Mossy the plush moose, in his blue flying helmet, goggles and white scarf, tucked into bed under a knitted Nordic blanket. Out the window, green northern lights glow over steaming black lava fields. A lantern glows beside the blue Bedtime Passport and an open travel journal with a map of Iceland.

nights.title: The Vault Inside the Mountain
nights.pronunciations: Fjord [FYORD], a glacier-carved inlet of the sea; Geirangerfjord [gay-RANG-er-fyord]; Svalbard [SVAHL-bar], the Arctic islands; elg [ELG], moose; God natt [GOO NAHT], good night.
nights.anchor: 800s to 1000s AD (Viking shipwrights building clinker-built wooden longships).
facts: Glacier-Carved Fjords:
Ice Age glaciers scraped out more than 1,000 deep fjords, long arms of the sea tucked between steep mountain cliffs.
The Global Seed Vault:
Deep inside a frozen mountain on Svalbard, the vault keeps more than a million backup packets of seeds from almost every country, to protect the world’s food.
Clinker Longships:
Viking shipbuilders overlapped thin planks like roof shingles. The ships were light and bendy, and strong enough to cross the Atlantic Ocean.
Midnight Sun:
In the far north of Norway, the summer sun stays up all night for weeks. In deep winter, it does not rise at all.
Moose Country:
Norway has many thousands of moose, which Norwegians call elg. They are the biggest animals in Norway’s forests.
story: Mossy is sitting on your pillow, reading a map upside down. He turns it the right way up. He turns it back.
“Tonight,” he whispers, “we are visiting a secret. A secret the whole world helps to keep. And, best of all, a country full of my cousins! Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land on the deck of a ferry gliding across dark green water. Cliffs shoot straight up on both sides, so high you have to tip your head all the way back. Waterfalls slide down the rock like silver ribbons. Everything smells of pine trees and cold, clean sea.
“This is a fjord [FYORD],” says Mossy, “a long arm of the sea tucked between mountains. Norway has more than a thousand of them.”
“Who dug them?” you ask. “Giants?”

“Ice!” says Mossy. “Long ago, rivers of ice called glaciers crept through these valleys. Slower than a snail, but strong as a bulldozer. They scraped the valleys deep. When the ice melted, the sea rushed in.”
Creak-splash. Creak-splash. A wooden ship slides past, with a carved dragon head at the front and a red-and-white striped sail.

“A Viking ship!” says Mossy. “See how the planks overlap, like fish scales? That made the ships light and bendy, so they rode over big waves instead of cracking. Ships like this sailed all the way across the Atlantic Ocean.”
On the shore, something big and brown steps out of the trees. It has long legs, a droopy nose, and wide, flat antlers.
Mossy gasps. “A moose! A real one!” He waves both hooves. The moose looks at Mossy’s helmet. Then at the goggles. Then it goes back to eating leaves.
“Norwegians call us elg [ELG],” Mossy says proudly. “There are thousands of us here. We’re the biggest animals in the forest.” He sighs happily. “He liked my helmet. I could tell.”

Then Mossy points far to the north. “Way up there, in summer, the sun forgets to go to bed! At midnight, it’s still up in the sky, like a guest who won’t go home. And in winter, it’s the opposite. The sun stays hidden for weeks, and the snow glows blue in the dark. But tonight, we’re going even farther. Goggles on!”

WHOOSH! Crunch. You land in snow on an island called Svalbard [SVAHL-bar]. The mountains look as if they have been dipped in sugar. Far away, a big white polar bear walks slowly along the shore. It does not even look up.

In the side of a snowy mountain, there is a narrow doorway that glows like a lantern. Mossy taps it three times. It swings open. Inside, a tunnel goes down, down, down into the mountain. It is so cold your breath makes little clouds.
At the end of the tunnel is a room lined with shelves. And on the shelves are boxes and boxes of little silver packets.

“Seeds,” whispers Mossy. “Wheat and rice. Corn and beans. More than a million packets, from almost every country in the world. This is the Seed Vault. If a farmer somewhere ever loses their seeds, in a flood or a dry year, they can get some back from here and start growing again.”
“It’s like a library,” you whisper, “but for seeds.”
“Exactly,” says Mossy. “And the frozen mountain keeps them cold, like a giant freezer.”

He hands you one tiny silver packet. It is light as a feather, but it feels very important. You set it gently on an empty shelf. Ka-chunk. Somewhere in the world, a future garden just got a little safer.
“Goggles on, sleepy explorer,” murmurs Mossy, and this time the wind that carries you is soft and warm.

You land in a fishing village where little red cabins stand on wooden legs, right over the water. Fishermen have slept in cabins like these for hundreds and hundreds of years. Yours has a slanted wooden ceiling and a fat feather comforter. The window is so close to the sea that you can hear the water lapping underneath. Lap, lap, lap.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size. He tucks the map under his chin like a tiny blanket. Outside, huge dark mountains stand around the fjord like sleeping giants. Somewhere in the forest, the big moose has folded his long legs and lain down in the moss.
“Far away, a million seeds are sleeping too,” Mossy says, pulling down his goggles. “Waiting to wake up someday. Whisper it with me: God natt [GOO NAHT].”
“God natt,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and listen to the water lapping under your little red cabin. Lap, lap, lap. Far away, one tiny seed is sleeping in the cold mountain. Picture the garden it will grow into, someday.
nights.alt: Mossy tucked under a dark blue quilt with snowflake stitching. Out the window, a steep mountain rises over a calm fjord lined with little red fishing cabins at dusk. A lantern, the Bedtime Passport and a journal with a map of Norway sit nearby.

nights.title: The Ship That Sailed for Twenty Minutes
nights.capital: Stockholm [STAHK-holm], built across 14 islands connected by 57 bridges.
nights.pronunciations: Vasa [VAH-sah], the 17th-century warship; fika [FEE-kah], the daily coffee-and-cake break; kanelbulle [KAH-nel-bool-eh], cinnamon bun; älg [ELL-ye], moose; Sov gott [SOHV GOT], sleep well.
nights.anchor: 1628 (the Vasa sinks in Stockholm harbor on its first voyage) and 1961 (it is raised from the harbor floor).
facts: The Almost-New Old Ship:
The royal ship Vasa sank on its very first trip in 1628. Cold Baltic mud kept it safe, and it was lifted out almost whole 333 years later.
No Shipworms Allowed:
Wood-eating shipworms cannot live in the Baltic Sea because it is not salty enough. That is why the Vasa did not get eaten away.
24,000 Islands:
The Stockholm Archipelago has more than 24,000 islands, islets, and rocks stretching out into the Baltic Sea.
Moose Crossing:
Sweden has hundreds of thousands of moose, called älg. Its yellow moose warning road signs are so popular that visitors sometimes buy copies to take home.
Fika:
Fika is a daily pause to put work down, share a warm drink and a treat like a cinnamon bun, and enjoy each other’s company.
story: Mossy is wearing a captain’s hat on top of his flying helmet. It keeps sliding down over his goggles.
“Tonight’s mystery,” he says from somewhere under the brim, “is this: how can a ship be almost four hundred years old and still look nearly new? Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land in a big, dim room, as tall as a church. In the middle, there is a ship. Not a toy ship. A real, enormous wooden ship, as long as five school buses parked in a row, with tall masts that reach up into the shadows.
“Welcome to Stockholm [STAHK-holm], in Sweden,” whispers Mossy, pushing up his hat. “And this is the Vasa [VAH-sah].”
You walk all the way around it. The ship is covered with carvings: lions with grumpy faces, mermaids with curly tails, and kings with tall crowns. Hundreds and hundreds of them.
“A king ordered this ship to be built almost four hundred years ago,” says Mossy. “He wanted the grandest ship on the whole sea. So they made it taller, and taller, and fancier, and fancier...”
“Uh-oh,” you say.

“Uh-oh is right,” says Mossy. “It was like stacking pancakes on a very small plate. On its very first trip, it sailed out of the harbor, a big gust of wind blew, and the ship tipped over. Glug, glug, glug. Down it went, after sailing for only about twenty minutes.”
“Twenty minutes!” you say. “That’s shorter than a bath!”
“And then,” says Mossy, “it waited at the bottom of the harbor, in the cold, soft mud. For three hundred and thirty-three years.”
“Why didn’t it rot away?”

Mossy leans close. “In most oceans, there are little sea creatures called shipworms. They eat wood the way you eat popcorn. But this sea isn’t very salty, and shipworms don’t like that. So they never came. The mud tucked the ship in like a blanket, and it just... waited.”

“Then one day, divers found it. They slid big cables underneath it and lifted it up, slowly, slowly, until it came out into the sunshine. Water poured out of it like a waterfall. And almost all of it was still the very same wood.”
You look closer. There are ropes still coiled up. A sailor’s leather shoe. Even wooden spoons.
“You can almost hear someone slurping soup,” says Mossy.
He taps his hat. “Now, after a mystery, every Swede knows exactly what you need. Fika [FEE-kah]!”
“Fika?”

“Every afternoon, Swedes stop what they’re doing for a warm drink and something sweet, with friends. No rushing. Just talking and chewing.” He hands you a warm, sticky cinnamon bun. “A kanelbulle [KAH-nel-bool-eh].”
You take a bite. Mossy takes a bite. There is now sugar on his goggles.

A little wooden ferry carries you out across the water. Stockholm is built on fourteen islands, joined by fifty-seven bridges. And beyond the city, the sea is sprinkled with islands. Twenty-four thousand of them! Some are big enough for a whole village. Some are just one rock, with room for one seagull and one very small pine tree. Mossy tries to count them and gives up at eleven.
Beside the road on the shore, you see a yellow sign shaped like a triangle, with a black moose on it.
Mossy stops. He stares. “That’s me,” he whispers. “There’s a sign. For me.”
“It means ‘watch out for moose,’” you say.

“Hundreds of thousands of moose live in Sweden,” says Mossy, beaming. “They call us älg [ELL-ye]. And people love these signs so much, they buy little copies to take home.” He stands next to the sign and poses. Click! You pretend to take his picture.

On the islands stand little cottages painted a deep strawberry red. “That red paint has a secret,” says Mossy. “Long ago, it was made from leftovers from an old copper mine. It soaks into the wood and protects it from rain and snow.”

The sun sinks low, turning the water the color of honey and rose petals. You step onto a quiet island and follow a path of soft pine needles to a little red cottage. Inside, a warm stove glows. You slide under a crisp sheet and a puffy blanket.
Outside, the seagulls have tucked their heads under their wings. The water laps at the rocks. Shhh. Shhh. Shhh. Far away, in its big quiet room, the old ship is resting too.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, takes off his captain’s hat, and pulls his goggles down. “In Norway, they say God natt. Here in Sweden, let’s say it another way. Whisper it with me: Sov gott [SOHV GOT]. It means sleep well.”
“Sov gott,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and drift in a little wooden boat between the islands. One rock with one seagull. One rock with one small pine tree. Let them float past, slowly, one at a time, until you lose count.
nights.alt: Mossy in bed under a red-and-white checked quilt. Out the window, red cottages dot little islands in a calm sea at sunset. A lantern glows on the nightstand, and an open journal shows a map of Sweden.

nights.title: The Quiet Kind of Brave
nights.pronunciations: Sisu [SEE-soo], quiet courage and grit; Sámi [SAH-mee], the Indigenous people of Lapland; Kalevala [KAH-leh-vah-lah], Finland’s epic poem; Hyvää yötä [HOO-vah OY-tah], good night.
nights.anchor: 1835 (Elias Lönnrot publishes the Kalevala, collected from songs village singers knew by heart).
facts: Land of 188,000 Lakes:
Finland has more than 188,000 lakes, and forests cover about three-quarters of the country.
Singing the Kalevala:
Long ago, Finnish singers kept their stories alive by singing them from memory. In 1835, the songs were collected into a book, the Kalevala.
The Power of Sisu:
Sisu is a Finnish word for quiet bravery: the inner strength to keep going when things get hard.
Reindeer Country:
In Lapland, herders, including many Sámi families, care for about 200,000 reindeer. Their wide hooves work like snowshoes.
Everyone’s Right:
Anyone in Finland may walk in the forest and pick wild berries and mushrooms, as long as they take care of nature.
story: Mossy is counting on his hooves. “Ninety... ninety-one... oh, bother. I lost count.”
“Count what?” you ask.
“Lakes! Tonight we’re visiting Finland. It has more than a hundred and eighty-eight thousand lakes. I only got to ninety-one. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land in a forest of tall pine trees and white birch trees. The first snowflakes of the year are drifting down. Through the trees, you see a lake shining like a dropped mirror. And past it, another. And another.
“If you counted one lake every second,” says Mossy, “it would take you more than two whole days. No sleeping. No snacks.” He shudders. “No snacks.”
Mossy sniffs the air and smiles. “Smell that? Pine and moss and cold water. This is my kind of forest. Moose live here too, you know.”
Across the water, a soft, rolling song floats through the trees. Two people are sitting on a log, holding hands, rocking back and forth as they sing, like a slow seesaw.

“Long ago, before most people had books, Finns kept their stories alive in songs,” Mossy whispers. “Songs about wizards, and magic, and sea monsters. People learned them by heart. Then a doctor named Elias Lönnrot walked from village to village and wrote them all down. He made them into a book called the Kalevala [KAH-leh-vah-lah]. In one of the stories, a wise old singer plays music so beautiful that all the animals of the forest come to listen.”
“Even the moose?” you ask.
“Especially the moose,” says Mossy.
You hold Mossy’s hoof, and rock, and hum along. It feels like being rocked in a very big cradle.
But the sky is turning pink. Mossy suddenly stands up. “The reindeer are on the other side of that hill. Let’s get there before dark! And tonight, let’s walk. I think you can do it.”
The hill is steep and rocky, and the wind is cold. Halfway up, your legs feel heavy. Mossy puffs. “Oof,” he says. “Antlers are heavy.”
You are tired too. But you take one step. Then another. Then another.
At the top, you both flop down in the snow, panting.

“Do you know what you just did?” says Mossy. “Finns have a special word for it: sisu [SEE-soo]. It means quiet bravery. Not the loud, roaring kind. It’s the little voice inside you that says, ‘I can take one more step.’”
“I had sisu?” you ask.
“Buckets of it,” says Mossy.

Below you, a whole herd of reindeer is moving through the snow, with antlers like walking bushes. A herder waves to you. She is Sámi [SAH-mee]. The Sámi people have lived in this cold northern land, called Lapland, and cared for reindeer for a very, very long time.
“There are about two hundred thousand reindeer here,” says Mossy. “A traffic jam in Lapland is made of antlers!”
A reindeer walks right past you. Its hooves are wide and flat, like snowshoes. “So it doesn’t sink in deep snow,” says Mossy. He looks down at his own hooves. “Mine are pretty good too.”

A little reindeer calf trots up and sniffs Mossy’s antlers. It has tiny fuzzy antlers of its own. “Look,” whispers Mossy. “We match!” The calf tilts its head at his flying helmet, as if to say, “Well, almost.”
The herder hands you a few tiny red berries called lingonberries. You pop one in your mouth. Sour! Your face scrunches up. Mossy tries one. His goggles fog up.
“In Finland, there’s a lovely rule,” says Mossy. “Anyone can walk in the forest and pick berries, as long as they take care of nature. The forest shares, and you take care of it.”

The night settles softly. At the edge of a lake so still it looks like glass, you find a log cabin with round wooden walls. Next to it is a tiny wooden sauna, a hot little room where Finns go to get toasty warm. “Finland has millions of saunas,” yawns Mossy. “About one for every two people.”
You climb into a wooden bunk piled high with soft wool blankets. Outside, a loon calls across the water. Ooooo-aaaah. The reindeer lie down in the snow, close together, warm as a family.
Mossy’s legs are tired too. He shrinks back to pillow size and flops down beside you. “You climbed a whole hill tonight,” he murmurs. “Whisper it with me: Hyvää yötä [HOO-vah OY-tah].”
“Hyvää yötä,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and feel how heavy your legs are after climbing that whole hill. Let them sink into the soft wool blankets. Out in the snow, the reindeer are snuggled close together, warm as a family. Snuggle in with them.
nights.alt: Mossy under a green patchwork quilt. Out the window, white birch trees stand beside a still lake under a lavender evening sky. A lantern, the Bedtime Passport and a journal with a map of Finland sit nearby.

nights.title: Bluetooth, Bricks, and Bedtime Stories
nights.pronunciations: Hygge [HOO-gah], cozy contentment; Billund [BIL-oond], where LEGO began; Odense [OH-den-seh], Hans Christian Andersen’s hometown; leg godt [LIE GOT], “play well”; Godnat [goh-NAHT], good night.
nights.anchor: Around 980 AD (King Harald Bluetooth builds round ring forts and unites Denmark) and 1932 (LEGO begins in Billund).
facts: King Harald Bluetooth:
About a thousand years ago, this Viking king joined the people of Denmark into one kingdom. Wireless Bluetooth is named after him, because it connects things together too.
The Birthplace of LEGO:
In 1932, a carpenter named Ole Kirk Christiansen began making toys in Billund. LEGO comes from leg godt, which means “play well.” A brick made in 1958 still snaps onto a brick made today.
Hans Christian Andersen:
Born in Odense, Andersen wrote The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, and The Princess and the Pea. He also loved cutting paper into fancy shapes.
Bicycle City:
In Copenhagen, about half of the people ride a bike to school or work, even in winter.
Hygge:
Hygge is the Danish word for being cozy together, with candles, warm socks, and quiet stories on long winter evenings.
story: Mossy is sitting on your pillow, clicking two plastic bricks together and looking very pleased with himself.
“Guess how old this red brick is,” he says.
“Ten years?” you guess.

“Nope. It was made in 1958. And this blue one was made last week. Watch.” Click! The bricks snap together perfectly. “Almost seventy years apart, and they still fit! Tonight we’re visiting the country where that happened. But first, a king with a very funny name. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land on a green hill in Denmark, a small country with lots of islands, between two seas. Down in the grass is a perfect circle, huge and round, with a high wall of earth all around it. It looks like a giant donut made of dirt.
“That’s a Viking ring fort,” says Mossy. “It was built about a thousand years ago by King Harald Bluetooth.”
“Bluetooth?” you giggle. “Was his tooth blue?”

“Maybe!” says Mossy. “Some people think he had one grayish-blue tooth. Harald was famous for bringing the people of Denmark together into one kingdom. And here’s the funny part. The Bluetooth that connects phones and headphones is named after him, because it joins things together, just like he did. Look closely at the little Bluetooth sign someday. It’s made from Harald’s initials, written in old Viking letters called runes.”
Inside the ring, people once lived in long wooden houses with curved walls, shaped like upside-down boats. You peek inside one. It smells of wood smoke and hay.
“Goggles on!”

WHOOSH! Now you are on a bumpy stone street in the town of Odense [OH-den-seh]. A boy with big feet and big ideas is sitting on a doorstep with a pair of scissors and a sheet of paper. Snip, snip, snip. Out of the paper comes a swan, a windmill, a lacy snowflake.
“That’s Hans Christian Andersen,” Mossy whispers. “When he grows up, he’ll write some of the most famous fairy tales ever. The Little Mermaid. The Ugly Duckling. And The Princess and the Pea.”
“The one with the pea under all the mattresses?” you ask.
“I’d feel it right away,” says Mossy. “Moose are very sensitive.” He tries to cut out a swan with his hooves. It comes out looking like a potato. The boy laughs, and so do you.

“One of his stories is about a little bird that everyone thought was an ugly duckling,” says Mossy. “But it was a baby swan all along. It just needed time to grow.” He holds up his potato-swan. “This one needs a LOT of time.”

WHOOSH! Now you smell fresh sawdust. You are in a carpenter’s workshop in a tiny village called Billund [BIL-oond]. A man named Ole is carving wooden toys: ducks, cars, little animals. He believes that children everywhere need time to play.
He needs a name for his toys. He thinks of two Danish words, leg godt [LIE GOT], which mean “play well.” He squishes them together. LEGO!

Years later, his company made plastic bricks with little bumps and tubes, so they click together tight. Mossy clicks his red and blue bricks one more time. “That’s why a brick from your grandma’s toy box still fits with yours.”

Ding-ding! A bicycle bell rings, and you are in Copenhagen [KOH-pen-hay-gen]. Bicycles are everywhere. Bikes with baskets. Bikes with bells. Bikes with a big box in front, full of giggling kids. “About half the people here ride bikes to school or work,” says Mossy, “even in the snow.” He tries to ride one. His knees stick out on both sides. He wobbles. He rings the bell anyway. Ding!

Evening comes, and the whole city glows candle-yellow. “Danes have a special word for this feeling,” Mossy says in a quiet, yawny voice. “Hygge [HOO-gah]. It means being cozy together. Candles on the table. Fuzzy socks. Something warm to drink. And stories with people you love.”
“So hygge is like a hug you can feel with your whole house?” you ask.
“That,” says Mossy, “is the best description I have ever heard.”

He leads you to a little cottage by the sea, with a roof made of golden straw. Inside, a candle flickers on white walls. You slip under a feather comforter as soft as a cloud. Outside, the waves roll gently onto the sand. Shhh. Shhh. The bicycle bells have all gone quiet.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, puts his two bricks on the nightstand, and blows out the candle. Puff.
“Whisper it with me,” he says, pulling down his goggles. “Godnat [goh-NAHT].”
“Godnat,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and feel the hygge all around you: fuzzy socks, a warm blanket, waves rolling softly onto the sand. In your dream, build anything you like, one quiet click at a time.
nights.alt: Mossy under a cream cable-knit blanket. Out the window, thatched-roof cottages line a cobblestone village street at night. A lantern glows beside the Bedtime Passport, and a journal shows a map of Denmark.

nights.title: The Turquoise Lakes and the Polar Bears Waiting for Ice
nights.pronunciations: Banff [BANF], the mountain national park; Churchill [CHUR-chill], the polar bear town; tire sur la neige [teer soor lah NEZH], maple taffy on snow; Unnukkut [oon-NOOK-koot], good evening and good night, in Inuktitut.
nights.anchor: 1885 (Canada protects the hot springs at Banff, the start of its very first national park).
facts: Turquoise Lakes:

Lakes in the Canadian Rockies, like Lake Louise and Moraine Lake, glow bright turquoise because glaciers grind rock into a fine powder called rock flour, which floats in the water and catches the sunlight.
Polar Bears:
Every fall, hundreds of polar bears gather near the town of Churchill, on Hudson Bay, waiting for the sea to freeze so they can walk out onto the ice.
Maple Syrup:
Most of the world’s maple syrup comes from Canada. In spring, people collect the sweet sap of maple trees and boil it down into syrup.
The Longest Coastline:
Canada has the longest coastline of any country in the world, touching three oceans: the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic.
Moose Country:
Canada has somewhere between half a million and a million moose living in its forests.
story: Mossy is holding a little jar of maple syrup up to the lamp. It glows gold, like sunshine in a bottle. He tips it, very slowly, and watches the syrup slide from one end to the other.
“Tonight,” he says, “we fly to the moosiest country I know. Hundreds of thousands of moose live there. Maybe even a million! And blue lakes, and polar bears, and something very sweet. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land on the rocky edge of a lake, high in the mountains. The air is cold and fresh and smells like pine trees. All around, tall gray mountains rise up, with snow on their tops and dark green forests on their sides. And the lake in front of you is blue. Not ordinary blue. Bright, glowing, milky turquoise, like a giant gemstone lying in the mountains.

“Banff [BANF], in Canada,” says Mossy, breathing in the cold pine air. “Glaciers up in the mountains grind the rocks into powder, as fine as flour. The powder floats in the lake, and the sunlight bounces off it, and makes this color.”

A red canoe is waiting at the shore. You climb in, and Mossy climbs in after you, very carefully, and the canoe wobbles, and then settles. You paddle out onto the turquoise water. The mountains are reflected upside down all around you.

And then, at the far edge of the lake, among the reeds, something big steps out of the trees. A mother moose, tall and brown, with long legs and a long nose. And right behind her, on wobbly legs, comes a baby moose.
The calf splashes into the shallow water. It slips. It sits down with a plop.

Mossy gasps. He sits up so straight the canoe rocks. “A baby!” he whispers, and puts a hoof over his heart. “Look how wobbly. Just learning.” The mother moose looks up from the water, chewing a mouthful of water plants. She looks at Mossy for a long moment. Mossy waves one hoof. Then she nudges her calf, and they both go back to munching.
“They’re shy,” says Mossy happily. “We’ll let them eat their dinner.”
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
Now you land inside a big, tall vehicle with huge wheels, like a bus on stilts, parked on a flat, snowy, rocky land beside a gray, frozen-looking sea.

And there, walking slowly across the snow, is a polar bear. A huge, creamy-white bear, with a long neck and big, furry paws as wide as dinner plates. And behind her, two cubs, round and fluffy, tumbling after her.

“Churchill [CHUR-chill],” whispers Mossy. “Every fall, polar bears gather here, waiting for the sea to freeze. When it freezes, they walk out onto the ice to find their food. We watch them from in here, safe and warm.”
Then the mother lies down, and the cubs snuggle into her big, warm belly, and all three close their eyes.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

The sun is setting when you land beside a little wooden cabin in a snowy forest of maple trees. Smoke is puffing from a chimney, and there’s a sweet, warm, delicious smell in the air. Inside, a big pan of maple syrup is bubbling on a fire.
“A sugar shack,” says Mossy. “And now, the best part.”

A man carries out a pot of hot, thick syrup, and pours it in long lines onto a tray of clean, fresh snow. It turns soft and chewy right away. He hands you a little wooden stick, and shows you how to roll the syrup up onto it, like a lollipop.
“Tire sur la neige [teer soor lah NEZH],” says Mossy. “Maple taffy on snow.”

Mossy takes a stick, and rolls up a big, big, big lump of taffy. He puts it in his mouth. He chews. And chews. And his teeth stick together. “Mmmf,” he says. “Mmmf mmf mmmf.” He tries to open his mouth. It won’t open. He points at the snow, very excited, and then flops backward into it, and makes a snow angel, still chewing, with his legs waving in the air.
“Mmmf mmf made for snow,” he says, which means moose are made for snow. You giggle and flop into the snow beside him and make a snow angel too.
As the sky gets dark, green lights begin to ripple and dance across the sky. The Northern Lights, swirling like green ribbons over the treetops.
You go into a log cabin, and climb into a bed with soft flannel sheets and a thick, puffy quilt, next to a crackling woodstove.

Outside, the Northern Lights are fading softly. The polar bears are curled up together by the frozen sea. The mother moose and her calf are resting in the forest by the turquoise lake. And the maple trees are standing quietly in the snow, their sweet sap dripping, drop by drop, into little buckets.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, and licks the last of the taffy off his lips. “People in Canada speak English and French, and many other languages too,” he says. “Up in the far north, near the polar bears, many people speak Inuktitut. Whisper it with me: Unnukkut [oon-NOOK-koot]. It means good evening, and good night.”
“Unnukkut,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and snuggle into the big, warm polar bear family by the frozen sea. Feel how soft and creamy her fur is. Breathe slow and deep, just like the sleepy cubs.
nights.alt: Mossy under a striped red, green and cream wool blanket in a log cabin. Out the window, a bright turquoise mountain lake sits below snowy peaks. An open journal shows a map of Canada and a polar bear stamp.

nights.title: The Country That Loves to Sing
nights.pronunciations: Toompea [TOHM-pay-ah], the limestone hill; Saaremaa [SAH-reh-mah], the largest island; Kaali [KAH-lee], the meteorite crater; põder [PUH-der], moose; Head ööd [HAY-ad URD], good night.
nights.anchor: 1200s to 1400s AD (Tallinn grows as a walled trading town of the Hanseatic League) and 1869 (Estonia’s first Song Festival).
facts: A Walled Old Town:
Tallinn has one of Europe’s best-preserved old towns, with stone walls and round watchtowers with pointy red roofs.
Bogs and Boardwalks:
About a fifth of Estonia is wetland. People cross the springy bogs on wooden boardwalks or in wide “bog shoes.”
The Kaali Crater:
Thousands of years ago, an iron meteorite from space crashed onto the island of Saaremaa. The crater is now a round, quiet lake.
The Song Festival:
Since 1869, Estonians have held a giant Song Festival. Every five years, tens of thousands of singers stand together on one huge outdoor stage.
Moose in the Forest:
About half of Estonia is covered in forest, and moose (põder) live there, along with bears, wolves, and lynx.
story: Mossy is sitting very still on your pillow, and for once, he isn’t being silly. He is humming. A slow, soft tune, deep and rumbly.
“Tonight,” he says softly, “we’re visiting a country that loves to sing. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land on bumpy cobblestones in Tallinn [TAH-lin], in the glow of old street lamps. Bells are ringing. All around you rise huge stone walls, with round towers topped by pointy red roofs, like witches’ hats.
“Can you count the towers?” asks Mossy.
You count. Five. Ten. Fifteen. Twenty! And more beyond.
“Tallinn is a very old town,” says Mossy. “Hundreds of years ago, ships sailed here from all over the sea to trade. Salt and cloth. Furs and honey. And the walls you see are still standing.”
You climb a hill called Toompea [TOHM-pay-ah] and look down at a maze of steep red rooftops and hidden little courtyards. It looks like a town from a storybook.
“Goggles on!” Now you are at the edge of a bog: a wide, wet, spongy land made of moss. Little dark pools look up at the sky like eyes. Red cranberries sparkle in the moss.
“How do you walk on a bog without sinking?” you ask.
Mossy grins and hands you a pair of big, flat bog shoes, like wooden snowshoes. You strap them on. Squelch. Bounce. Squelch. Bounce. The ground wobbles like a big green trampoline.

Mossy doesn’t need bog shoes. “Moose hooves spread out wide,” he says proudly, bouncing along beside you. “Perfect for bogs. Estonia is full of moose, you know. They call us põder [PUH-der].” He bounces a little higher. Boing. Boing. Squelch. He sinks up to his knees. “Well. Mostly perfect.”

A ferry carries you to a big island called Saaremaa [SAH-reh-mah]. Wooden windmills stand along the shore, their arms turning slowly in the wind. In the woods, you find a perfectly round lake, ringed with whispering trees.

“This is Kaali [KAH-lee],” says Mossy. “Thousands of years ago, a big iron rock from space zoomed down and crashed right here. KABOOM! It made a giant round hole. Then rain filled it up, and now it’s the quietest lake you’ve ever seen.”
You toss in a pebble. Plink. The ripples spread wide and slow. Mossy looks up at the sky, a little nervously. “Don’t worry,” he says. “That was a very, very long time ago.”
“And now,” says Mossy, “the best part. You need your voice for this one.”

He flies you back across the sea to a huge outdoor stage beside the water. It is shaped like a giant seashell. “Every five years, Estonians have a Song Festival,” says Mossy. “Tens of thousands of singers stand on this stage together, in colorful clothes, and even more people sing along from the grass. They’ve been doing it for more than a hundred and fifty years. When they all sing at once, you can hear it all across the city.”
“That many people?” you whisper. “All singing together?”
“Estonians love to sing,” says Mossy. “Some people call it the singing country. Ready? Hum with me.”
You hum a slow, soft tune, and Mossy hums along in his deep, rumbly moose voice. In the quiet night air, it feels as if the whole country is humming with you.

The night is very still now. You find a wooden farmhouse surrounded by sweet-smelling juniper bushes. You slide under a soft woolly blanket. Outside, a breeze whispers through the birch trees. Out in the bog, a moose has lain down in the soft moss, and the dark pools are reflecting the very first stars.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size and settles beside you. “Whisper it with me,” he murmurs. “Head ööd [HAY-ad URD].”
“Head ööd,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and hum Mossy’s slow, soft tune, quieter and quieter, until it is only a whisper. Then let the hum float away over the dark pools of the bog, where the very first stars are shining.
nights.alt: Mossy under a white quilt with embroidered flowers. Out the window, the stone walls and pointed red-roofed towers of an old town glow at night. A lantern, the Bedtime Passport and a journal with a map of Estonia sit nearby.

weeks.map_alt: Storybook map on old parchment of the top of the world, from Canada across Iceland to Scandinavia, under green northern lights. Seven numbered red pins mark Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Canada and Estonia, joined in order by a dotted blue route.

nights.title: Breakfast for the Baby Elephants
nights.capital: Nairobi [nye-ROH-bee] (from a Maasai phrase meaning “cool water”)
nights.pronunciations: Maasai [mah-SYE], the people who live on the southern plains; Maasai Mara [mah-SYE MAH-rah], the famous grassland reserve; shúkà [SHOO-kah], the bright checked cloth many Maasai wear; Noto enkewarie sidai [NOH-toh en-keh-WAH-ree-eh see-DYE], have a good night, in Maa, the Maasai language.
nights.anchor: 1977 (Daphne Sheldrick founds the elephant nursery that becomes the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust in Nairobi).
facts: The Great Migration:
Every year, more than a million wildebeest, along with zebras and gazelles, walk in a giant loop through Tanzania and Kenya, following the rain to find fresh green grass.
The Elephant Nursery:

In Nairobi, the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust has cared for hundreds of baby elephants who lost their families. Keepers feed them milk from giant bottles and help them go back to the wild when they are grown.
Weaver Bird Nests:
Male weaver birds tie real knots in blades of grass, using only their beaks, to build round hanging nests.
Giraffe Tongues:
A giraffe’s dark, bluish-purple tongue is about as long as your arm. It wraps around thorny branches to pull off the leaves.
Elephant Rumbles:
Elephants talk in rumbles so low that people can barely hear them. Other elephants can feel them through the ground, far away.
story: Mossy is sitting on your pillow, holding a baby bottle. It is the biggest baby bottle you have ever seen. It is almost as big as he is.
“Tonight,” he whispers, “we are making breakfast for someone very big who is also very small. Goggles on!”

You hold your finger-circles over your eyes. The Passport flashes. Mossy tucks the giant bottle into his scarf, takes one deep breath, and puffs up to pony size like a balloon. You climb onto his warm, wide back. WHOOOOSH! Out the window you go, south over the sea, toward the warm air.
When you land, the air is warm and smells of dry grass and dust. The sun presses on your shoulders like a warm hand. Mossy pushes up his goggles and fans himself with his ear.
“Phew,” he says. “Moose are made for snow. Welcome to Kenya, explorer.”
All around you is grass, golden and waving, as far as you can see. Here and there stands a tree with a flat top, like an umbrella. It is an acacia [ah-KAY-shah] tree.
Then you hear it. A low drumming, like a thousand tiny drums. Mossy lifts you onto his back and flies you up, up, up into the sky.
Below you, the whole plain is moving.

“The Great Migration,” Mossy whispers. Wildebeest, with shaggy beards and curvy horns. Zebras, in their stripy pajamas. Gazelles, bouncing like popcorn. “More than a million animals,” says Mossy. “Every year they walk in a giant circle, following the rain. Wherever the rain goes, fresh green grass pops up. And wherever the grass goes, they go.”
“It looks like a parade,” you say.
“The longest parade on Earth,” says Mossy.
He lands softly under an acacia tree. “Let’s rest in the shade for a minute,” he says, and settles down with a happy sigh.
Something up above goes *slurp*.
A giraffe is looking down at him. It sticks out a long, dark, bluish-purple tongue, as long as your arm, and licks Mossy’s goggles.
“Well,” says Mossy, wiping them. “Hello to you too.” You laugh and laugh, and the giraffe goes calmly back to its breakfast.
“Giraffes use those long tongues to pull leaves off thorny branches,” Mossy says. “And look up there.”
Hanging from the branches are little round nests made of grass, like upside-down baskets. A small yellow bird is tying a knot with its beak.
“A weaver bird,” says Mossy. “He ties real knots. No hands!” The weaver bird hops over to Mossy’s antlers and looks at them very carefully. “Oh no you don’t,” says Mossy. “These are not for rent.”
The sun climbs higher. “Now,” says Mossy, holding up his giant bottle, “breakfast! Goggles on!”
WHOOSH! You land at the edge of a city called Nairobi [nye-ROH-bee]. Its name comes from a Maasai phrase that means “cool water.” Mossy sighs happily. “Cool water. Now that’s my kind of name.”

Here, in a big green yard, is a nursery. Not for babies like you. For baby elephants! Some are so small they are only as tall as you are. Some wear little blankets to keep warm. They lost their families, so kind people called keepers look after them until they are big enough to go back to the wild.

A keeper smiles and hands you a bottle full of warm milk. A tiny elephant trots right up to you, flapping her ears. She wraps her trunk around the bottle, and around your hand, and drinks. Glug, glug, glug. The whole bottle is gone in a few seconds.
“She says thank you,” says Mossy. The baby elephant puts her trunk on Mossy’s nose and sniffs. Mossy sniffs back. Friends.

Now the day is ending, and the sky turns orange and pink, like the inside of a peach. Out on the plains, the big elephants rumble to each other, low and soft, so low you feel it more than hear it. “That’s how they say good night,” Mossy whispers. “Other elephants can feel it through the ground, far, far away.”

You come to a tent with a canvas roof under a tall acacia tree. Inside there is a wide bed, and on top is a soft red-and-blue checked blanket, like the shúkà [SHOO-kah] cloth that many Maasai people wear. You snuggle under it. The crickets begin their slow, sleepy song.

Far away, the wildebeest have lain down in the grass. The giraffe folds her long legs. The weaver bird is tucked inside his knotted nest. And back at the nursery, the little elephants are asleep in their blankets, with their keepers sleeping right beside them.

Mossy gets smaller and smaller, until he is pillow-sized again and tucked under a corner of the checked blanket. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Noto enkewarie sidai [NOH-toh en-keh-WAH-ree-eh see-DYE]. It means have a good night, in the Maasai language.”
“Noto enkewarie sidai,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and feel the elephants’ good-night rumble, low and soft, coming up through the ground and into your bed. Hmmmm. Let it rock you, slow and gentle, like a baby elephant asleep in her blanket.
nights.alt: Mossy under a red-and-blue checked blanket. Out the window, flat-topped acacia trees stand on a golden savanna at sunset. A lantern glows, and an open journal shows a map of Kenya and a giraffe.

nights.title: The Footprints in the Ash
nights.capital: Dodoma [doh-DOH-mah] (the largest city is Dar es Salaam)
nights.pronunciations: Kilimanjaro [kil-ih-man-JAR-oh], Africa’s tallest mountain; Laetoli [lye-TOH-lee], where the footprints were found; Ngorongoro [en-gor-on-GOR-oh], the giant crater; Usiku mwema [oo-SEE-koo MWEH-mah], good night, in Swahili.
nights.anchor: 1978 (Mary Leakey’s team uncovers footprints at Laetoli, pressed into volcanic ash about 3.6 million years ago).
facts: Mount Kilimanjaro:
Africa’s tallest mountain (about 19,341 feet) is a sleeping volcano that stands all by itself. Even though it is close to the equator, there is snow and ice on top.
The Oldest Footsteps:
At Laetoli, scientists found a trail of footprints made about 3.6 million years ago by early human relatives walking on two feet. Soft volcanic ash hardened like cement and kept them safe.
Ngorongoro Crater:
Long ago, a giant volcano fell in on itself and left a huge green bowl. Today about 25,000 large animals live inside, including zebras, hippos, lions and rare black rhinos.
Chimpanzee Toolmakers:
In Gombe, scientist Jane Goodall watched wild chimpanzees for many years and discovered that they make tools, like sticks for fishing termites out of their mounds.
Swahili:
Swahili is spoken by many millions of people across East Africa. “Jambo” [JAHM-boh] means hello.
story: Mossy has a pan of mud on his lap. He presses his hoof into it. Squish. He lifts it up and looks at the print.
“How long do you think this footprint will last?” he asks.
“Until morning?” you guess.
“Tonight,” says Mossy, “we’re going to see footprints that have lasted for millions of years. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! When you land, your nose goes cold. The wind whistles past your ears. Wheeee-oooo. Your breath makes little clouds. Under your feet there is something white and crunchy.
“SNOW!” shouts Mossy. He buries his whole nose in it and blows. PFFFT! Snow flies everywhere and lands on his antlers like frosting. “Oh, I’ve missed you, snow!”
You are standing on top of Mount Kilimanjaro [kil-ih-man-JAR-oh], the tallest mountain in Africa. The sun is just coming up, and far below, the clouds look like a fluffy white floor.

“Kilimanjaro is a sleeping volcano,” says Mossy, shaking snow off his helmet. “And it stands all by itself. No mountain brothers or sisters. Down at the bottom, it’s warm, with banana farms and monkeys. But up here, near the top, there’s snow and ice, even though we’re close to the middle of the Earth, where it’s usually hot.”
“A mountain with a snow hat,” you say.
“A very tall hat,” says Mossy. He takes one last snowy sniff. “Goodbye, snow,” he sighs. “I’ll miss you most of all. Goggles on!”
WHOOSH! You land on a flat, dusty plain. A scientist is kneeling on the ground with a soft brush. Swish, swish, swish. She is brushing away the dust very gently, like tucking in a baby.
“Jambo [JAHM-boh],” she says, which means hello, and she points.
In the hard gray rock there are footprints. Real footprints. A long trail of them, walking side by side. Some are big. Some are small.

“A very, very long time ago,” Mossy whispers, “a volcano puffed out a soft gray ash, like flour. Then it rained a little, and the ash got squishy, like wet sand. Early relatives of people walked across it on two feet. Then the sun baked the ash hard, like cement. And their footprints stayed. For three million, six hundred thousand years.”
You kneel down. One little footprint is just about the size of yours.
You put your hand next to it. Your hand is almost the same size. You think about someone, long, long ago, walking along on a soft gray afternoon, maybe holding a grown-up’s hand.
“Someone walked here with their family,” you whisper.

“Just like you and me,” says Mossy. He sets one hoof down beside the trail, very carefully, without touching. Then he looks at his hoof. Then at the footprints. “Mine would look very silly next to these.”
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

Now you are on the edge of a giant green bowl. It is so big that the zebras at the bottom look like sprinkles on a cake. “This is Ngorongoro [en-gor-on-GOR-oh] Crater,” says Mossy. “Long ago, a huge volcano fell in on itself and left this bowl. Now about twenty-five thousand big animals live inside. It’s like a zoo that nobody built.”

You fly down, low and quiet. Hippos yawn in a pond. A big gray rhino munches grass, with a little bird riding on its back. “Black rhinos are very rare,” whispers Mossy. “This bowl helps keep them safe.” Far away, across the plain, a lion family naps in the sun.

Near the lake stand hundreds of pink flamingos, each one balancing on one skinny leg. Mossy tries it. He lifts one leg. Wobble. He lifts another. Wobble, wobble. He tips over, SPLOOSH, into the soft mud. The flamingos don’t even look up. You giggle all the way to the top of the crater.

The sky turns the color of apricots. On the rim of the crater stands a little stone cottage with a fire crackling inside. You climb into a deep bed under a thick wool blanket. Through the window, a cool mist fills the crater like milk in a bowl.

Down below, the hippos sink low in their pond. The flamingos tuck their heads under their wings. The rhino lies down in the tall grass, with the little bird still on its back. The lions have curled into one sleepy pile. And far away, the old footprints lie quietly under the stars, where they have waited for more than three million years.
Mossy shrinks down to bedtime size and burrows into the wool blanket until only his antlers show. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Usiku mwema [oo-SEE-koo MWEH-mah].”
“Usiku mwema,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and watch the cool mist fill the crater, like milk filling a bowl, slowly, slowly, until the whole world is soft and white and quiet.
nights.alt: Mossy under a colorful patterned blanket. Out the window, snowcapped Mount Kilimanjaro rises against the night sky. A lantern, the Bedtime Passport and a journal with a map of Tanzania sit nearby.

nights.title: The River That Never Finds the Sea
nights.pronunciations: Okavango [oh-kah-VAHN-goh], the river and its delta; mokoro [moh-KOH-roh], a narrow canoe pushed with a pole; Pula [POO-lah], rain, and the country’s cheer; Robala sentle [roh-BAH-lah SEN-tleh], sleep well, in Setswana.
nights.anchor: 2014 (the Okavango Delta becomes the 1,000th place on UNESCO’s World Heritage List).
facts: The River That Stays:
The Okavango River never reaches the sea. It spreads out across the dry Kalahari sand into a giant maze of channels, lagoons and islands called the Okavango Delta.
Floods in the Dry Season:
Rain falls far away in the highlands of Angola, and the water travels so slowly that the delta floods in the middle of Botswana’s dry season.
Land of Elephants:
Botswana has more elephants than any other country. Elephants are good swimmers and can use their trunks like snorkels.
Pula Means Rain:
In a dry land, rain is treasured. “Pula” means rain in Setswana. It is the country’s motto, a cheer at big gatherings, and the name of its money.
Reed Frog Chorus:
Tiny painted reed frogs, about as long as your thumb, sing in the delta at night with a sound like little bells.
story: Mossy is sitting on your pillow with a cup of water and a little pile of sand. He pours the water onto the sand. It disappears.
“Where did it go?” he asks. “Tonight, we’re visiting a river that never reaches the sea. It just... goes into the sand. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land with a soft swish. You are sitting in a long, narrow canoe, gliding across water so clear you can see little silver fish darting between the roots. All around you are tall green reeds, and round lily pads, and white and purple water lilies. The air is warm and still, and a dragonfly lands on the edge of the canoe, as blue as a jewel.

“This canoe is called a mokoro [moh-KOH-roh],” says Mossy. A man stands at the back of it, pushing you along with one long pole. Push, glide. Push, glide. He smiles and says, “Dumela [doo-MEH-lah].” That means hello. “Dumela!” you say back.
Mossy looks at the canoe. The canoe is very narrow. Mossy is very not.
“I’ll swim,” he says, and slides into the water. Splash!

“Welcome to the Okavango [oh-kah-VAHN-goh] Delta, in Botswana,” says Mossy, paddling beside you with just his nose, his goggles and his antlers poking out. “The Okavango River starts far away, where it rains a lot. It flows and flows, all the way here, into the middle of a big, dry desert. And then, instead of finding the sea, it spreads out into a giant maze of water, like fingers on a hand.”
“So the desert gets a swimming pool,” you say.
“The biggest one around,” says Mossy.
Then he takes a big breath. And he disappears. Gloop.
You wait. The water is still. The man with the pole raises his eyebrows.
SPLOOSH! Mossy pops up, and on top of his antlers there is a whole bunch of water lilies, like a flower crown. He is chewing happily.
“Moose can dive for water plants,” he says, with his mouth full. “Back home, I dive for them in the lakes. These ones are delicious.”
You giggle so much the canoe wobbles.

Then the man with the pole points. On the far bank, a family of elephants is walking into the water. The big ones go first. The little ones follow, holding tails with their trunks. Deeper and deeper they go, until only their trunks are sticking up out of the water, like snorkels. One little elephant slips all the way under. For a moment, you see only the tip of its trunk, wiggling. Then up it pops, blowing bubbles.

“Botswana has more elephants than any other country in the world,” says Mossy. “And look, they swim too!” He paddles a little closer. A young elephant blows a spray of water right over his helmet. Pfffft!
“Well,” says Mossy, dripping. “I suppose I deserved that.”
On a sandy island, people are gathered in a circle, singing. Someone shouts, “PULA [POO-lah]!” and everybody cheers.
“Pula means rain,” Mossy explains. “Here in the dry land, rain is a treasure. So they shout it when they’re happy. It’s even the name of their money.”
You cup your hands and shout it too. “PULA!” And everybody cheers again. Mossy stomps his hooves. “PULA!” he booms, so loudly that a heron flaps up out of the reeds.

The sun sinks low, and the sky turns copper and gold. The whole delta shines like a mirror. One by one, the water lilies fold their petals, closing up for the night like tiny sleepy hands. Somewhere in the dark, a hippo lets out a big, grumbly sigh. Hrrrmmph.

The mokoro glides up to a little island, where a tent stands on a wooden platform under a big leafy tree. Mossy climbs out of the water and shakes himself off like a dog. Shake, shake, shake. You get a little wet. The man with the pole waves good night and glides away into the gold.
Inside the tent is a bed with soft linen sheets. You slide under them. Through the mesh windows, a warm breeze brings the smell of wet grass and wild sage.
And then the music begins. Tink. Tink-tink. Tinkle-tink. Hundreds of tiny painted reed frogs, no bigger than your thumb, are singing across the water, like a whole field of little bells.
Out on the riverbank, the elephants stand close together, sleeping on their feet. The water lilies are closed tight. The river goes on, slowly, slowly, sinking into the sand.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, still a tiny bit damp, and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Robala sentle [roh-BAH-lah SEN-tleh]. It means sleep well.”
“Robala sentle,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and listen to the reed frogs singing like tiny bells. Tink. Tink-tink. Feel your canoe drifting, push and glide, push and glide, while the water lilies fold up their petals for the night.
nights.alt: Mossy under a blue blanket with a wavy water pattern. Out the window, starlit channels and lily pads spread across a wide delta. An open journal shows a map of Botswana.

nights.title: The Drummers of Gishora and the Spring Where the Nile Begins
nights.pronunciations: Gishora [gee-SHOH-rah], the drum sanctuary; karyenda [kar-YEN-dah], the great sacred drum; Rutovu [roo-TOH-voo], where the Nile’s farthest spring bubbles up; Tanganyika [tan-gahn-YEE-kah], the long, deep lake; Ijoro ryiza [ee-JOH-roh REE-zah], good night, in Kirundi.
nights.anchor: 2014 (the ritual dance of the royal drum of Burundi is added to UNESCO’s list of the world’s treasured traditions).
facts: The Royal Drummers:
Burundi’s drummers play huge drums carved from tree trunks. They carry them on their heads, then play them in a thundering circle while they leap and dance.
The Nile’s Farthest Spring:
A little spring near Rutovu, in the hills of Burundi, is often called the farthest source of the Nile, the longest river in Africa. A small stone pyramid marks the spot.
Lake Tanganyika:
Lake Tanganyika is the longest freshwater lake in the world and the second deepest.
Tea Hills:
Burundi’s green hills are covered in tea gardens, planted in neat rows that curve around the slopes.
Kirundi:
Kirundi, the language of Burundi, is a close cousin of Kinyarwanda, the language of neighboring Rwanda.
story: Mossy is drumming. He’s got an upside-down pot on his lap, and he’s playing it with two wooden spoons. BOOM. Boom-boom. BOOM. Boom-boom.
“Tonight,” he says, still drumming, “we’re going to hear the most amazing drummers in the world. So I’m warming up. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land on a green hilltop, under tall, shady trees. The hills roll away all around you, green and soft, like a crumpled green blanket. And in the middle of a wide, grassy clearing stand the drums.

Big, tall wooden drums, painted in red and white and green, each one carved from a single tree trunk, with a skin stretched tight across the top. They’re lined up in a big half circle. And in the middle is one more drum, the biggest of all.
“Gishora [gee-SHOH-rah], in Burundi,” says Mossy, still tapping a spoon against his leg to a beat only he can hear. “This is a sanctuary for drums. And here come the drummers.”

Walking up the hill in a long line are the drummers, dressed in red and white and green. And each one is carrying a huge drum, balanced on top of his head. Walking, singing, with the drums on their heads, not even using their hands.
They set the drums down in the circle. They lift their sticks. And then:
BOOM.

The ground shakes. BOOM. BOOM. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM. All the drums, all together, so loud you can feel it in your tummy and your toes. The drummers take turns leaping into the middle of the circle, jumping high in the air, kicking and spinning, then running back to their drums. BOOM-BOOM. BOOM. The sound rolls out over the green hills like thunder.

Mossy is so excited, he can’t sit still. He’s tapping his hooves. He’s nodding his head. And then he can’t help it. He takes out his wooden spoons and his little pot, and joins in, right on the end of the row. Boom-boom-BOOM. Tink, tink, tink.
The big drums go BOOM. Mossy’s pot goes tink.
The drummers look over at him. They smile. And on the next beat, all together, they stop. Silence. And Mossy, all by himself, goes: tink.
Everyone bursts out laughing. The drummers laugh so hard they have to lean on their drums. You roll over in the grass, giggling. And Mossy takes a very proud bow.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

Now you land on a hillside, in soft, misty air. In front of you is a little stone pyramid, and beside it, coming out of the ground, a tiny spring of clear water, bubbling up between the stones and running off down the hill in a little stream.

“Rutovu [roo-TOH-voo],” says Mossy. “Have you heard of the great river Nile? It’s the longest river in Africa. And this tiny spring is often called its farthest beginning. From right here, the water travels thousands of miles, all the way across Africa, to the sea.”
You dip your finger in the cold, clear water. Then you put a leaf in the little stream and watch it float away, down the hill.
“Maybe it’ll get all the way to the sea,” you say.
“Maybe it will,” says Mossy.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
The sun is setting when you land on a golden beach, beside a huge, long lake, so long you can’t see the end. Mountains rise up on the far side, turning purple.
“Lake Tanganyika [tan-gahn-YEE-kah],” says Mossy. “The longest freshwater lake in the world.”
Out on the lake, fishing boats are heading out for the night, with lanterns glowing on their fronts, like floating stars.
You go to a little guesthouse on the hill above the lake, and climb into a bed with a soft cotton sheet and a warm woolen blanket.
Outside, the lanterns are twinkling on the lake. The drums are resting on the hilltop. And the tiny spring is still bubbling, sending your leaf away on its long, long journey.

Mossy sets his spoons and his pot down very quietly, and shrinks back to pillow size. “People in Burundi speak Kirundi,” he murmurs. “Whisper it with me: Ijoro ryiza [ee-JOH-roh REE-zah]. It means good night.”
“Ijoro ryiza,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and follow your little leaf as it floats down the stream, around the rocks, past the green hills, slowly, slowly, on its long, long journey to the sea.
nights.alt: Mossy under a green striped blanket. Through an open window, green hills and thatched huts glow in a warm sunset. A lantern, the Bedtime Passport and a journal with a map of Burundi sit nearby.

nights.title: The Sand That Rusted
nights.pronunciations: Namib [NAH-mib], the desert along the coast; Sossusvlei [SOSS-us-flay], the valley of red dunes; welwitschia [vel-VIT-chee-ah], a desert plant with only two leaves; Ka lale po nawa [kah LAH-leh poh NAH-wah], sleep well, in Oshiwambo.
nights.anchor: At least 55 million years ago (the Namib Desert has been dry for so long that it is often called the oldest desert on Earth).
facts: The Oldest Desert:
The Namib Desert has been dry for at least 55 million years. That is why it is often called the oldest desert on Earth.
Rusty Red Dunes:
The dunes at Sossusvlei are some of the tallest in the world, and some are more than 1,000 feet high. The sand is red because it has a thin coat of iron that has rusted.
Fog to Drink:
On many mornings, cool fog rolls in from the Atlantic Ocean. Some desert beetles do a headstand so the fog drips down their backs and into their mouths.
Desert Elephants:
Namibia’s desert elephants can go for days without drinking. They dig holes in dry riverbeds to reach water, and other animals drink there too.
The Two-Leaf Plant:
A welwitschia grows only two leaves in its whole life. Some of these plants are more than 1,000 years old.
story: Mossy is holding up an old nail. It is orange and rough.
“Rust,” he says. “When iron gets wet and waits a long time, it turns orange. Now, here’s the mystery. How can a whole desert of sand turn red like this? Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land, and your feet sink. Soft, cool sand pours over your toes like sugar.

It is very early in the morning. All around you rise giant dunes, curving hills of sand, glowing red and orange in the first light. Some are taller than the tallest building in your town. Much taller.
“The Namib [NAH-mib] Desert, in Namibia,” says Mossy, wiggling his hooves deeper into the cool sand. “It has been a desert for millions and millions of years. It might be the oldest desert on Earth.”
You scoop up a handful of sand. Up close, every grain is red.
“Each grain of sand has a thin coat of iron,” says Mossy. “And over a very long time, the iron rusted. Just like my nail. So the whole desert...”
“Rusted!” you say.
“A rusty desert,” says Mossy. “I love it.”
You decide to climb a dune. It is very steep. Every time you take a step, the sand slides back a little. Step, slide. Step, slide. Your legs burn. But you keep going, and at last you reach the top.
The desert stretches out in waves of red and gold, like a frozen ocean.

“Now,” says Mossy, “the best way down.” He sits on the sand. He pushes off. And he slides all the way down, antlers first, bottom bumping, ears flapping. WHEEEEEEE! At the bottom, he ends up with his head buried in the sand and his back legs waving in the air.
Giggling, you slide down after him.
“You know,” says Mossy, popping his head out, “this desert gets almost no rain at all. So how do animals drink? Watch.”

A soft white fog is rolling in from the sea, cool and damp, like a wet cloud. On top of a dune, a small black beetle stops. It leans forward. It sticks its bottom up in the air. It is doing a headstand!
Tiny drops of fog gather on its back, roll down, down, down, and drip right into its mouth.

“That’s how it drinks,” whispers Mossy. “It catches fog.” He tries a headstand too. His antlers stick in the sand. He stays there. “Could you... give me a little push?” You push. He flops over onto the sand with a big POOF of red dust.
Near the rocks, you find the strangest plant. It has only two long leaves, twisted and curly like ribbons.
“A welwitschia [vel-VIT-chee-ah],” says Mossy. “It grows just two leaves in its whole life. And some of these are more than a thousand years old. They drink the fog too.”
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
You land in a dry, rocky riverbed. Walking toward you, slow and quiet, is a family of elephants.
“Desert elephants,” Mossy whispers. “They can go for days without a drink.”
The biggest elephant stops. She digs in the dry sand with her foot and her trunk. Dig, dig, dig. Deeper. And deeper. And then, at the bottom of the hole, water begins to shine.

She drinks. Her baby drinks, then squirts a little water over its own head to cool off. Mossy watches, fanning his ears. “Good idea,” he says. And after the elephants move on, a little bird hops down and drinks too. Then a jackal. Then a family of zebras.
“She dug a well for everyone,” you whisper.
“That,” says Mossy, “is a very good neighbor.”

The sun slides down behind the dunes, and the red sand turns purple, then dark blue. The air grows cool. You walk to a little lodge made of stone, and climb into a low wooden bed with a heavy linen quilt.
Outside, there are no city lights for miles and miles. So the stars come out. First one. Then ten. Then millions, pouring across the sky like a glowing river of sand.

A soft wind sighs over the dunes, smoothing away your footprints, one by one. Out in the dunes, the beetle has tucked itself into the cool sand. The elephants rest in the riverbed, standing close. The welwitschia sleeps with its two curly leaves, waiting for tomorrow’s fog.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, shakes one last bit of sand out of his ear, and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Ka lale po nawa [kah LAH-leh poh NAH-wah]. It means sleep well, in Oshiwambo, the language spoken in more Namibian homes than any other.”
“Ka lale po nawa,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and count the desert stars as they come out. First one. Then ten. Then too many to count. Let the soft wind smooth away your footprints, one by one.
nights.alt: Mossy under a rust-orange blanket. Out the window, tall red sand dunes lie under the Milky Way. An open journal shows a map of Namibia.

nights.title: A Name for a Baby Gorilla
nights.pronunciations: Virunga [vih-ROON-gah], the chain of volcano mountains; Kwita Izina [KWEE-tah ee-ZEE-nah], the gorilla naming celebration; Umuganda [oo-moo-GAHN-dah], community work day; Ijoro ryiza [ee-JOH-roh REE-zah], good night, in Kinyarwanda.
nights.anchor: 2005 (Rwanda holds its first Kwita Izina, a yearly celebration to name baby mountain gorillas).
facts: Land of a Thousand Hills:
Rwanda is a small, green country so full of hills that it is nicknamed the Land of a Thousand Hills.
The Gorilla Comeback:
In the early 1980s, only about 250 mountain gorillas lived in the Virunga volcanoes. Thanks to scientists and rangers who protect them, there are now more than 1,000 mountain gorillas in the wild.
Kwita Izina:
Every year, Rwanda holds a big celebration to give names to the baby gorillas born that year, just as families name a new baby in front of friends.
Umuganda:
On the last Saturday of every month, people all over Rwanda work together to plant trees, clean streets and fix paths.
Gorilla Beds:
Every evening, gorillas build a brand-new nest of leaves and branches to sleep in.
story: Mossy is chewing on a pencil. On his lap is a piece of paper covered with scribbles and crossed-out words.
“I’m trying to think of a name,” he says. “For a baby. A very small, very hairy baby. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land, and cool rain patters on your cheeks. Pit, pat, pit. All around you, green hills roll away into the mist, one after another, like a giant, rumpled green blanket.
Mossy takes a deep breath. “Ahhh. Cool air. Rain. This feels like home.”
“Welcome to Rwanda,” he says. “People call it the Land of a Thousand Hills.” He tries to count them. He gets to four. The rest are hiding in the clouds.
It is Saturday morning, and the whole town is outside. Children and grown-ups are sweeping paths, picking up litter and planting trees.
“This is Umuganda [oo-moo-GAHN-dah],” says Mossy. “On the last Saturday of every month, everybody works together to take care of their town.”

A girl in a yellow raincoat hands you a tiny tree. You dig a hole, set the tree inside and pat the soil down around it. Pat, pat, pat. The girl gives you a thumbs-up. Everyone claps. Mossy claps too, with his hooves. Clop, clop, clop.
“There,” says Mossy. “Now part of Rwanda will grow a little greener, because of you. Goggles on!”

WHOOSH! You land on the side of a tall, misty mountain, in a forest of bamboo. This is one of the Virunga [vih-ROON-gah] volcanoes. A ranger in a green uniform walks ahead of you, very quietly. He holds a finger to his lips. Shhh.
He gently moves some leaves aside.
In a little clearing sits a family of mountain gorillas.

There is a mother, chewing on a stalk of wild celery. There are two young gorillas, rolling and tumbling in the ferns like puppies. And in the middle sits the biggest gorilla of all, with a patch of silver fur across his back.

“A silverback,” Mossy whispers. “He’s the dad. He’s very strong, but very gentle. He only eats plants. Just like me.” Mossy looks at the silverback. The silverback looks at Mossy. “He might even be a little bigger than me,” says Mossy. “Well. Almost.”
The young gorillas stop tumbling and stare at Mossy’s antlers. One of them stands up and pats its chest, pok-pok-pok, very small and very proud.
Mossy pulls his goggles down, very politely, as if he is trying to look smaller.

“A long time ago, there were only a few mountain gorillas left,” he whispers. “But scientists and rangers worked very hard to keep them safe. Now there are more than a thousand. That’s a big, happy comeback.”

Then something tiny tumbles out of the ferns. A baby gorilla! It has fuzzy black hair sticking up on its head and big, shiny brown eyes. It toddles right up to Mossy, grabs the end of his white scarf and tugs.
Mossy freezes. The baby tugs again. Then it wraps the scarf around its own head, like a hat, and sits down, looking very proud.
You clap your hand over your mouth so you don’t laugh out loud. Mossy’s eyes crinkle behind his goggles.
The mother gorilla reaches over and gently takes the scarf back. She hands it to Mossy. Then she scoops up her baby.

“Every year,” Mossy whispers, “Rwanda has a big celebration called Kwita Izina [KWEE-tah ee-ZEE-nah]. People give names to all the baby gorillas born that year. The names have meanings, like ‘hope’ or ‘friend.’”
He looks at his scribbly paper. “What would you name this one?”
You think very hard. Then you whisper your name into Mossy’s big ear.
“Perfect,” he says, and writes it down.

The mist rolls down the mountain, soft and white, tucking the forest in. The gorillas start to build their beds. They bend branches, pile up leaves and pat them flat, making a brand-new nest, just like they do every single night.

The ranger smiles and leads you back down the trail. You walk to a little stone cottage at the edge of the forest. A fire glows in the fireplace. You slide under a thick, fluffy blanket. Outside, the rain has stopped, and the little tree you planted is drinking it all up, and the whole mountain smells of wet leaves and fresh earth.
Up in the bamboo, the silverback lies down in his nest. The mother curls around her baby. And the baby falls asleep, still dreaming about a soft white scarf.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, folds up his paper and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Ijoro ryiza [ee-JOH-roh REE-zah]. Remember it from Burundi, next door? Cousins.”
“Ijoro ryiza,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and build your own nest, just like the gorillas do. Bend the soft branches. Pile up the leaves. Pat them flat, pat, pat, pat. Now curl up inside it, safe and warm.
nights.alt: Mossy under a black-and-red patterned blanket. Out the window, misty green volcanoes and bamboo glow in the night. An open journal shows a map of Rwanda and a mountain gorilla.

nights.title: The Mountain with a Tablecloth
nights.capital: Three capitals: Pretoria [pree-TOR-ee-ah], Cape Town and Bloemfontein [BLOOM-fon-tayn].
nights.pronunciations: protea [PROH-tee-ah], the national flower; fynbos [FAYN-boss], the bushy plants of the Cape; Sawubona [sah-woo-BOH-nah], hello, in isiZulu; Lala kahle [LAH-lah GAH-hleh], sleep well, in isiZulu.
nights.anchor: 1982 (two pairs of African penguins settle at Boulders Beach and start a colony that grows into the thousands).
facts: Table Mountain:
This flat-topped mountain above Cape Town is about 3,500 feet tall. Wind often pushes a cloud over the top that spills down the sides, and people call it the “tablecloth.”
The Cape’s Flowers:
The tip of South Africa is home to more than 9,000 kinds of plants, and most grow nowhere else. The king protea, the national flower, can be as big as a dinner plate.
Boulders Beach Penguins:
A colony of African penguins lives among giant round boulders near Cape Town. They bray like donkeys, swim fast, and it all started with just two pairs of penguins.
Twelve Languages:
South Africa has twelve official languages, including isiZulu, isiXhosa, Afrikaans, English and South African Sign Language.
Big Wild Parks:
