Kruger National Park is one of the biggest wildlife parks in Africa, home to elephants, lions, leopards, rhinos and buffalo.
story: Mossy has spread a white napkin over a pile of pillows. He smooths it out very carefully.
“There,” he says. “A mountain, with its table set. Tonight we’re visiting a real one. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land on a windy hilltop. The air smells salty and fresh, and far below you, the sea sparkles blue.
Right in front of you stands a mountain. But its top isn’t pointy. It is flat, as flat as a kitchen table, stretching across the sky.
“Welcome to Cape Town, in South Africa,” says Mossy. “And that is Table Mountain.”
As you watch, a fluffy white cloud slides over the flat top. It spills down the sides, slowly, slowly, like a big white tablecloth. But it never reaches the bottom. It just melts away into the air.
“The wind pushes the cloud up and over,” says Mossy. “People here call it the tablecloth.”
Mossy opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue as the cloud drifts past. “I’m trying to taste the tablecloth,” he explains. It tastes like nothing. He looks a little disappointed.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH! You land right on top of the mountain.

All around you are bushy plants with tiny leaves, and flowers of every color. Pink, orange, yellow, red. From up here, you can see the whole city, the beaches and the wide blue ocean all around. “These bushes are called fynbos [FAYN-boss],” says Mossy. “More than nine thousand kinds of plants grow here at the tip of Africa, and most of them grow nowhere else.”
He points his nose at a huge pink flower, as big as a dinner plate. “A king protea [PROH-tee-ah]. South Africa’s national flower.”
Mossy sniffs it. The protea tickles his nose. “Ah... ah... AH-CHOO!” His sneeze is so big that his goggles fly off and land on a bush. A little bird hops over and looks into them.
You laugh until your tummy hurts.
“Goggles on,” says Mossy, getting them back. “Quick, before that bird flies off with them!”
WHOOSH! You land on a beach of soft white sand, between giant round boulders as big as houses. And everywhere, walking between the rocks, are little black-and-white birds.
“Penguins!” you shout.
“African penguins,” says Mossy. “And listen.”
One penguin lifts its head, and out comes a sound. HEE-HAWWW!
“It sounds like a donkey!” you say.
“That’s just how they talk,” Mossy chuckles. “A long time ago, only two penguin couples came to live on this beach. Now there are thousands. People here protect them and keep their nests safe.”
One penguin dives into the water. Whoosh! On land, penguins waddle. But in the sea, they zoom like little rockets.

Mossy tries to walk like a penguin. He holds his front legs stiff at his sides. He waddles. Left, right, left, right. A penguin stops and stares at him. Then it waddles right behind him. Then another one. Soon, Mossy has a whole line of penguins following him down the beach.
“I’m the leader now,” he whispers proudly.
A boy on the beach waves at you. “Sawubona [sah-woo-BOH-nah]!” he calls. That means hello in isiZulu, one of South Africa’s twelve official languages. You wave back and call, “Sawubona!”

The sun sinks into the sea, pink and gold. The penguins tuck themselves into their burrows under the bushes and murmur softly to their chicks. You come to a little white cottage above the beach and climb into a bed piled with soft cotton quilts.

The waves roll in, slow and soft. Shhh. Shhh. The big boulders still hold the warmth of the sun. Up on the mountain, the tablecloth cloud is still pouring slowly over the edge in the dark, tucking the proteas in. Far away, across all of Africa, the elephants and gorillas and flamingos are sleeping too.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he murmurs. “Lala kahle [LAH-lah GAH-hleh]. It means sleep well.”
“Lala kahle,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and watch the soft white tablecloth cloud spill over the mountain, slowly, slowly, until it tucks you in too. Shhh go the waves. Shhh.
nights.alt: Mossy under a quilt with pink flowers. Out the window, a white cloud spills over flat-topped Table Mountain above the sea. An open journal shows a map of South Africa.

weeks.map_alt: Storybook map on old parchment of eastern and southern Africa, with little pictures of elephants, giraffes and mountains. Seven numbered red pins mark Kenya, Tanzania, Botswana, Burundi, Namibia, Rwanda and South Africa, joined in order by a dotted blue route.

nights.title: The Train with a Bird’s Beak
nights.pronunciations: Shinkansen [SHEEN-kahn-sen], the bullet train; Fuji [FOO-jee], the tallest mountain in Japan; onsen [OHN-sen], a hot spring bath; Oyasumi nasai [oh-yah-SOO-mee nah-SYE], good night, in Japanese.
nights.anchor: 1964 (the first bullet train line opens between Tokyo and Osaka).
facts: The Kingfisher Train:
Early bullet trains made a loud BOOM when they rushed out of tunnels. An engineer who loved birdwatching gave one train a long nose shaped like a kingfisher’s beak, and it became much quieter.
Mount Fuji:
Japan’s tallest mountain is a sleeping volcano about 12,388 feet tall. It last erupted more than 300 years ago, in 1707.
Snow Monkeys:
In the snowy mountains of Nagano, wild Japanese macaques warm up in natural hot spring pools.
Hot Spring Baths:
Japan has thousands of hot springs, warmed by heat deep underground. A bath in one is called an onsen.
Sleeping on Tatami:
In a traditional Japanese inn, you sleep on a soft futon mattress laid on floor mats woven from rush grass, called tatami.
story: Mossy is sitting very still on the windowsill. On the tip of his hoof, a shiny coin is standing up on its edge. He is holding his breath.
“Shhh,” he whispers. “I’m practicing being smooth. Tonight we ride the smoothest train in the world. Goggles on!”
You make circles with your fingers and hold them over your eyes. The Passport flashes. Mossy grows and grows, and you climb onto his warm, wide back. WHOOOOSH! Your bedroom folds up like a paper map.
When you land, you are standing on a long, shiny platform. Cool air smells of rain and rice crackers. A bell chimes, ding-dong, and a sleek white train glides up beside you, as quiet as a cat.
“Welcome to Japan,” says Mossy, pushing up his goggles. “And this is the Shinkansen [SHEEN-kahn-sen]. People call it the bullet train, because it is so fast.”
The front of the train is long and pointy. It looks like a bird’s beak.

“That’s on purpose,” says Mossy. “Long ago, when these trains zoomed out of mountain tunnels, the air went BOOM! like a giant popping a paper bag. So an engineer who loved watching birds thought about the kingfisher. A kingfisher dives into the water to catch fish, and hardly makes a splash. He gave the train a nose like a kingfisher’s beak. And the boom went away.”
“A train that copied a bird,” you say.
“The smartest ideas often come from animals,” says Mossy proudly.
You climb aboard. Mossy climbs aboard too, antlers first. Clunk. He tilts his head. Clunk. He tries again, sideways, and squeezes through the door with a pop.
The train slides away, faster and faster, and yet it feels as calm as a boat on a pond. Mossy takes out his coin, stands it on the windowsill and holds his breath again.
It doesn’t fall. Not even a wobble.
“SMOOTH,” Mossy whispers, delighted.
Out the window, a huge mountain rises up, with a white cap of snow on its pointy top.

“Mount Fuji [FOO-jee],” says Mossy. “It’s a volcano. But it has been sleeping for more than three hundred years. Just like you will be soon.” You giggle. Fuji looks like a giant scoop of vanilla ice cream sitting on the clouds.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
Now you land in snowy mountains. Snowflakes drift down, soft as feathers. Your breath makes little clouds. And in front of you, steam is rising from a warm pool among the rocks.
Sitting in the pool, with snow on their heads, are monkeys! Fluffy, pink-faced monkeys, soaking up to their chins with their eyes half closed.
“Snow monkeys,” whispers Mossy. “When it’s cold, they warm up in the hot spring. Deep under Japan, the ground is very hot, and it warms the water.”
A baby monkey paddles over and stares at Mossy’s antlers. Then it reaches up and pats his nose. Pat, pat.
Mossy looks at the warm water. He looks at the monkeys. “Could I just dip one hoof?” he asks.

The monkeys shuffle over and make room. Mossy lowers one hoof into the pool. Then another. Then all four, and then his whole big moose body, until the water sloshes over the edge in a warm wave. SPLOOSH! The monkeys hop onto the rocks and stare at him.
“Sorry,” says Mossy, with only his nose and antlers sticking out. “Ahhhh. But this is wonderful.”
You laugh so hard that snow falls off a branch onto your head.

The sun sets, and the snowy mountains turn pink, then blue. You walk to a wooden inn with a curvy roof and paper lanterns glowing at the door. A kind woman bows and slides open a door made of thin wood and white paper.

The floor is covered in soft mats woven from grass, called tatami. They smell sweet, like a summer field. In the middle of the room, a thick, cloud-soft mattress called a futon is waiting right on the floor, with a crisp white quilt on top.
You snuggle in. Mossy curls up on a tatami mat beside you, still a tiny bit steamy.

Outside the window, a stone lantern glows in a little moss garden. Snow falls softly on the pines. The snow monkeys are huddled together in one warm, fluffy ball. Far away, the bullet train rests in its station, its long beak pointed toward morning. And Mount Fuji sleeps under the stars, just as it has for three hundred years.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Oyasumi nasai [oh-yah-SOO-mee nah-SYE].”
“Oyasumi nasai,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and sink into the warm hot spring with the snow monkeys, right up to your chin. Watch the snowflakes drift down, one by one, softer than feathers, and melt before they touch you.
nights.alt: Mossy under an indigo tie-dye blanket. Out the window, snowcapped Mount Fuji rises behind bamboo and a stone lantern. An open journal shows a map of Japan.

nights.title: The King’s Alphabet and the Warm Floor
nights.pronunciations: Hangul [HAHN-gool], the Korean alphabet; Jeju [JEH-joo], the volcano island; ondol [OHN-dohl], a floor warmed from underneath; Annyeonghi jumuseyo [ahn-NYUNG-hee joo-moo-SEH-yo], sleep well, in Korean.
nights.anchor: 1443 (King Sejong the Great creates Hangul, an alphabet made so that everyone could learn to read).
facts: An Alphabet for Everyone:

Long ago, reading Korean meant learning thousands of hard characters. In 1443, King Sejong made Hangul, a simple alphabet so everyone could learn to read. Some letters are shaped like the mouth and tongue making the sound.
A Palace with Guardians:
Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul was first built in 1395. Stone statues of the haetae, a legendary lion-like creature, stand guard outside.
A Tunnel Made by Lava:
On Jeju Island, a river of lava once flowed underground. It left behind Manjanggul, a lava tube cave several miles long, with a stone pillar about 25 feet tall inside.
Warm Floors:
For hundreds of years, Korean homes have used ondol: warm air from a fire travels through tunnels under the floor, so the whole floor becomes cozy and warm.
The Sea Women of Jeju:
On Jeju, women called haenyeo dive into the sea without air tanks to gather shellfish and seaweed. Some keep diving into their eighties.
story: Mossy is drawing in the air with his hoof. A line. A circle. A little square.
“What are you writing?” you ask.
“I’m trying to make a letter shaped like my mouth,” says Mossy. He makes an O with his lips. “Hmm. Tonight we’re visiting the country with the cleverest alphabet in the world. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land in front of a huge wooden gate with a curvy roof. The roof is painted in stripes of green, red, blue and gold, like a giant wooden rainbow. Beside the gate sits a stone creature with a curly mane and a big toothy grin.

“A haetae,” says Mossy. “An old legend says it guards the palace.” Mossy leans close to the haetae. The haetae grins at him. Mossy grins back, with all his teeth. “I think we’re friends,” he whispers.
“Welcome to Seoul, in South Korea,” he says. “This palace is more than six hundred years old. And a very kind king once lived here. His name was King Sejong.”
You walk into a quiet courtyard, where the stones are smooth and warm from the sun.

“Long ago,” says Mossy, “if you wanted to read in Korea, you had to learn thousands and thousands of hard letters. It took years and years. So lots of people never learned. King Sejong thought that wasn’t fair. So he and his scholars made a brand-new alphabet, called Hangul [HAHN-gool]. It was so simple that people said a clever person could learn it in one morning.”
“Just one morning?” you say.

“And here’s the best part,” says Mossy. “Some of the letters are shaped like your mouth and tongue when you say the sound.” He shows you a letter shaped like a little box. “That one is M. See? Your lips make a box when you say mmmm.”
You press your lips together. Mmmm. It’s true!
Mossy tries a letter too. He opens his mouth very wide to make a big round O. A butterfly flies in. Mossy freezes. The butterfly flies out again.
You have to sit down on the warm stones, you are giggling so much.
“Goggles on,” says Mossy, a little pink under his fur. WHOOSH!
Now you land on an island in the sea, where black rocks meet bright blue water. The wind smells of salt and oranges.
“This is Jeju [JEH-joo] Island,” says Mossy. “It was made by a volcano. And under our feet there is a secret tunnel. Follow me.”
You climb down some steps into a long, dark cave. It is cool inside, like a cellar. The walls are smooth and rippled, as if they melted once.

“They did melt,” whispers Mossy. “A long, long time ago, a river of hot lava flowed through here, underground. The outside cooled and turned hard, like a pipe. Then the lava ran out, and left this tunnel behind. It is called a lava tube.”
At the end of the tunnel stands a tall stone pillar, taller than a house. It looks like a frozen waterfall made of rock.
“Hello!” you call. Hello, hello, hello, says the cave.
Mossy takes a deep breath. “HELLO!” he booms, in his deep moose voice. HELLO, HELLO, HELLO, HELLO, rumbles the cave, for a very long time. Mossy looks pleased. “It likes me.”
Back up in the sunshine, you watch women in black wetsuits floating on the waves. One by one, they dive down and pop back up with shells and seaweed.
“The haenyeo,” says Mossy. “The sea women of Jeju. They dive without any air tanks, just by holding their breath. Some of them are grandmothers!” One diver waves at you. You wave back.
The sun sets, orange and pink, over the sea. You walk to a little wooden house with a curvy tiled roof, called a hanok. You take off your shoes at the door and step inside.
The floor is warm. Warm like a cat that has been sleeping in the sun.

“Ondol [OHN-dohl],” says Mossy. “Under the floor there are tunnels, and warm air from a fire flows through them. So the whole floor turns into a big, cozy heating pad.” He lies down flat on his tummy. “Oh,” he sighs. “Oh, my.”
You unroll a soft cotton mattress right onto the warm floor and snuggle under a thick quilt. The warmth soaks up through the mattress, into your back, into your toes.

Outside, the wind rustles the leaves of an old ginkgo tree, and golden leaves shaped like little fans drift down into the courtyard. Out at sea, the divers have come home to rest. The haetae stands guard at the palace gate. And deep under the island, the lava tube is dark and quiet.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size and lies flat on the warm floor again, with a long, happy sigh. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Annyeonghi jumuseyo [ahn-NYUNG-hee joo-moo-SEH-yo]. It means sleep well.”
“Annyeonghi jumuseyo,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and feel the warm ondol floor under your back. Let the warmth soak up into your shoulders, your tummy, all the way down to your toes, while golden ginkgo leaves drift down like little fans.
nights.alt: Mossy under a rainbow patchwork quilt. Out the window, curved tile roofs and pine trees sit under a crescent moon. An open journal shows a map of Korea.

nights.title: Heaven Lake on the Snowy Mountain and the Waterfalls of the Fragrant Hills
nights.pronunciations: Paektu [PAYK-too], the tall volcano; Chonji [CHUN-jee], Heaven Lake; Myohyang [MYOH-hyahng], the Fragrant Mountains; gayageum [GAH-yah-goom], the long Korean zither; Jal jayo [JAHL jah-YOH], sleep well, in Korean.
nights.anchor: Around 946 (a huge eruption of Mount Paektu forms the great crater that later fills with water and becomes Heaven Lake).
facts: Mount Paektu:
Mount Paektu, on the border between North Korea and China, is the highest mountain in all of Korea. It is a volcano.
Heaven Lake:
At the top of Mount Paektu, a round crater lake called Heaven Lake is surrounded by jagged peaks. It stays frozen for much of the year.
An Old Story:
Old Korean stories say Mount Paektu is where the very first Korean kingdom began.
The Fragrant Mountains:
The Myohyang Mountains are named for the sweet smell of their forests. They are full of streams and waterfalls.
The Gayageum:
The gayageum is a long wooden instrument with many strings, plucked with the fingers. Its sound is soft and flowing, like water.
story: Mossy is sitting on the floor with a long wooden ruler across his lap, and he’s stretched rubber bands along it, from one end to the other. He plucks them, one by one, very gently. Plink. Plonk. Plunk.
“It’s a gayageum [GAH-yah-goom],” he says. “Well. Almost. Tonight we’ll hear a real one. And we’ll visit a lake right at the top of a snowy mountain. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land on a mountaintop, in the cold, bright air. There’s snow all around, white and crunchy. And below you, in the middle of a huge, round bowl of jagged, snowy peaks, is a lake. It’s deep blue, and perfectly round, and so still that the sky is reflected in it like a mirror. At its edges, it’s still frozen, white and glittering.

“Mount Paektu [PAYK-too], in North Korea,” says Mossy, his breath puffing out in little clouds. “It’s the highest mountain in all of Korea. It’s a volcano, and a very long time ago, the top of it blew off, and left a giant crater. And the crater filled up with water.”
“Chonji [CHUN-jee],” he says. “Heaven Lake.”
It really does look like heaven. Blue water, white snow, and the jagged peaks all around it, like the points of a giant crown.
“There’s an old, old story,” says Mossy, “that Korea’s very first kingdom began here, on this mountain.”
And then Mossy notices the snow. Deep, fresh, soft snow, all around his hooves. His eyes go wide. He wiggles his ears.
“Snow!” he says. “I love snow! Moose are made for snow!”

“And do you know what snow is best for?” he says. “Snow moose.” So he builds one. He rolls a big snowball for the body, and a smaller one for the head, and a long one for the nose. He pats it all smooth. Then he looks around for something to make antlers. There are no trees up here. So he takes off his own goggles and sets them on the snow moose’s head instead.
He steps back to admire it. It’s a very good snow moose. It has a long nose, and goggles, and a very serious face.

Then he turns to you, very proudly, and says, “Isn’t it wonderful? Now I can see...” He stops. He blinks. “Actually,” he says, “I can’t see much at all. My goggles are on the snow moose.” He pats around in the snow with his hoof, looking for them, and bumps his nose right into the snow moose, and the whole head falls off, plop, onto his hooves.
You giggle so much you topple over into the soft snow. Mossy puts his goggles back on, and the snow moose’s head back on too, a little bit crooked.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

Now you land in a forest of tall pine trees, in the hills. The air smells sweet and fresh and piney. A stream is rushing past over mossy rocks, and ahead of you, a waterfall is pouring down a cliff, in a long white ribbon, into a clear green pool.
“The Myohyang [MYOH-hyahng] Mountains,” says Mossy. “The name means fragrant mountains, because the forests smell so sweet.”

You follow a little path up beside the stream. There are more waterfalls, one after another. A small one, splashing like a tap. A tall, thin one, like a silver thread. A wide one, falling in steps, like a staircase of water. Little birds hop along the rocks, and a squirrel with tufted ears watches you from a branch.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

The sun is setting when you land in a warm little room with a wooden floor that’s heated from underneath, so your feet feel toasty. And in the corner, a woman is sitting on a cushion with a long wooden instrument across her lap, strung with many silky strings.
“A real gayageum,” whispers Mossy.

The woman plucks the strings with her fingers, and bends them, and the music comes out soft, and flowing, like water running over stones. Rising and falling. Plink, and ripple, and sigh. It sounds like the waterfalls you just saw.
Mossy listens with his eyes closed. He doesn’t even try to play along. He just listens.
You climb into a bed on the warm floor, a thick, soft mattress with a smooth cotton sheet and a padded quilt, embroidered with pink and white flowers.

Outside, the waterfalls are splashing softly in the fragrant mountains. Heaven Lake is lying still and round, high on its mountain, with the stars reflected in it. And the little snow moose is standing on the mountaintop, with its head a little bit crooked, slowly getting covered in fresh snow.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size. “Remember Annyeonghi jumuseyo, from South Korea?” he says. “Here’s another way to say good night in Korean, the way you’d say it to a friend. Whisper it with me: Jal jayo [JAHL jah-YOH]. It means sleep well.”
“Jal jayo,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and listen to the gayageum, soft and flowing, like water running over stones. Plink. Ripple. Sigh. Let the music carry you down the mountain, one waterfall at a time.
nights.alt: Mossy under a blue quilt. Out the window, a round, deep blue crater lake sits among snowy mountain peaks at night. A lantern glows, and an open journal lies on the bed.

nights.title: The Temple on the Hill and the Real-Life Dragons
nights.capital: Jakarta [jah-KAR-tah] (a new capital city, Nusantara, is being built on the island of Borneo)
nights.pronunciations: Borobudur [boh-roh-boo-DOOR], the great stone temple; Komodo [koh-MOH-doh], the dragon island; gamelan [GAH-meh-lahn], an orchestra of gongs and bells; Selamat tidur [seh-LAH-maht TEE-door], sleep well, in Indonesian.
nights.anchor: About 800 AD (Borobudur is built on the island of Java from about two million blocks of volcanic stone).
facts: Seventeen Thousand Islands:
Indonesia is made of more than 17,000 islands, stretched across warm seas along the equator.
Borobudur:
This giant stone temple on Java is the largest Buddhist temple in the world. Its walls are carved with more than 2,600 picture panels, and 72 bell-shaped stone domes called stupas sit on top.
Komodo Dragons:
The world’s biggest lizards live on Komodo and a few nearby islands. They can grow about 10 feet long and taste the air with their long yellow tongues.
Gamelan Music:
A gamelan is an orchestra of bronze gongs, bells and drums. Its music sounds shimmery, like drops of water on metal.
Marching Ducks:
On Bali, farmers lead flocks of ducks through the rice fields. The ducks eat bugs and weeds, which helps the rice grow.
story: Mossy has built a tower out of pillows on your bed. A big square pillow on the bottom, then a smaller one, then a smaller one, and a tiny round cushion on top.
“A temple,” he says proudly, just as it wobbles and falls over. Flump. “Hmm. Tonight we’re visiting one that has stood for more than a thousand years. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land on a hilltop just as the sun is coming up. Mist lies in the valleys like soft white blankets. All around, green volcanoes poke up through the clouds.
And in front of you is a mountain made of stone.

Mossy tilts his head all the way back to see the top. “Borobudur [boh-roh-boo-DOOR], on the island of Java, in Indonesia,” he says. “People built this temple more than a thousand years ago, out of about two million stones. It is the biggest Buddhist temple in the whole world.”

You start to climb. The temple is built like a giant stepped cake, with walkways going around and around each layer. And on the walls there are pictures carved in stone. Ships with big sails. Elephants. Monkeys. Dancers. Birds in the trees.

“Every picture tells part of a story,” whispers Mossy. “There are more than two thousand six hundred of them. If you walked all the way around every level, you would read the whole thing, like the pages of a book.”
“A stone storybook,” you say.

At the very top, the air is cool and quiet. Rows and rows of stone bells sit in circles, each one with little diamond-shaped windows. They are called stupas. Inside each one, a stone statue sits peacefully, looking out over the valley.
You sit down too, very still, and watch the sun turn the mist from pink to gold. Mossy sits beside you, very still as well. It is the quietest he has ever been.
“Goggles on,” he whispers at last. WHOOSH!
Now you are on a wooden boat, bobbing on turquoise water beside a dry, rocky island. A ranger in a green hat stands at the front, holding a long forked stick.
“This is Komodo [koh-MOH-doh] Island,” says Mossy, “home of the Komodo dragon.”
“A real dragon?” you whisper.
“A real lizard,” says Mossy. “The biggest lizard in the whole world. Look, on the beach.”
Lying on the warm sand is a lizard longer than your bed. Its skin is bumpy and gray, like an old tree. It lifts its head, and out slides a long, forked yellow tongue. Flick. Flick.
“It tastes the air with its tongue,” the ranger says quietly. “That is how it smells things, even far away. We stay on the boat and give it lots of room.”
The dragon flicks its tongue toward Mossy. Flick. Mossy sticks out his own big pink moose tongue and waves it about. Flap, flap.
The dragon stares at him. Then it turns around and slowly crawls away into the shade, as if to say, that is not how you do it.
You giggle, and the little boat rocks. Even the ranger chuckles.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
You land on the island of Bali, on a narrow path between wide, flat rice fields, full of water that shines like green mirrors. Little frogs plop into the puddles. Plip. Plop.
Then you hear it. Quack. Quack-quack. A farmer is walking along the path, holding a stick with a little white flag. And behind him, in a long, neat line, march a hundred ducks.
“They eat the bugs and weeds in the rice fields,” says Mossy. “The ducks help the rice, and the rice helps the ducks.”
Mossy falls into line behind the very last duck. He waddles. He quacks, quietly. The farmer looks back, sees a moose in a flying helmet marching with his ducks, and smiles a huge smile.
As the sun goes down, soft music drifts over the fields. Bong. Ting-ting. Bong. It sounds like raindrops falling on bells.
“Gamelan [GAH-meh-lahn],” says Mossy. “A whole orchestra of gongs and bells.”

You follow the music to a little wooden house with a tall, pointed roof. Inside is a bed with a white net hanging around it like a soft tent, and pillows covered in blue-and-white batik cloth. You slide under the thin cotton sheet.

Outside, a warm rain begins to fall on the big banana leaves. Pat. Pat-pat. The ducks are tucked together in their pen, their heads under their wings. On Komodo, the dragon has crawled into its cool, sandy burrow. And up on the hill, the stone bells of Borobudur stand quietly in the dark, as they have for more than a thousand years.

Mossy shrinks down, small enough to fit inside the white net with you, and pulls his goggles over his eyes. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Selamat tidur [seh-LAH-maht TEE-door]. It means sleep well.”
“Selamat tidur,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and sit very still at the top of the stone temple, as still as Mossy was. Listen to the warm rain on the banana leaves. Pat. Pat-pat. Pat.
nights.alt: Mossy under a dark blue batik blanket with gold flowers. Out the window, the bell-shaped stone stupas of a great temple stand above misty hills. An open journal shows a map of Indonesia.

nights.title: The Stairs to the Clouds and the Big-Eyed Friend
nights.pronunciations: Ifugao [ee-foo-GAH-oh], the mountain people who built the rice terraces; Palawan [pah-LAH-wahn], the island with the underground river; tarsier [TAR-see-er], a tiny big-eyed animal; Magandang gabi [mah-gahn-DAHNG gah-BEE], good evening (word for word, “beautiful night”), in Tagalog.
nights.anchor: Hundreds of years ago (the Ifugao people carve rice terraces into the mountains of northern Luzon, which they still farm today).
facts: More Than 7,600 Islands:
The Philippines is made of more than 7,600 islands in the warm Pacific Ocean.
Stairs for Rice:
In the mountains of Luzon, the Ifugao people built giant stair-step rice fields by hand. Water flows from each step to the next one down.
A River Under a Mountain:
On Palawan, a river flows for miles through a dark limestone cave before it reaches the sea. Visitors float through it in small boats.
The Tarsier:
The tarsier is one of the world’s smallest primates and fits in your hand. Each of its eyes is about as big as its whole brain, and it can turn its head almost all the way around.
Firefly Trees:
In some mangrove forests, thousands of fireflies gather in the same trees at night and blink their lights.
story: Mossy has pulled his goggles down, and he is making his eyes very, very wide behind them. He blinks at you slowly. Blink. Blink.
“What are you doing?” you ask.
“I’m practicing being a tiny animal with enormous eyes,” he says. “Tonight we’re going to meet one. But first, some very big stairs. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land high on a mountain, in cool, misty air. And all around you, the mountains are covered in giant green steps. Step after step after step, curving around the hills, all the way down into the valley and all the way up into the clouds.

“The Philippines!” says Mossy, gazing at the green steps going up and up into the clouds. “These are rice terraces. The Ifugao [ee-foo-GAH-oh] people built them by hand, hundreds of years ago, with stone and mud, so they could grow rice on the steep mountains. And they still farm them today.”
Water trickles from the top step to the next one, and the next, and the next, like a slow, sparkly slide. Trickle, trickle, splash.

A girl with a basket of rice seedlings waves to you from one of the steps. She shows you how to push the little green plants into the soft mud. Squish. You plant one. Squish. You plant another. She grins and gives you a thumbs-up.
Mossy tries to climb up one step. His front hooves go up. His back hooves stay down. He is stuck, half on one step and half on the other, like a moose bridge.
“Could you... help?” he asks. You push. He scrambles up, with muddy knees and a very proud face.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
Now you are sitting in a little wooden boat, at the mouth of a giant cave. The water is clear and green. A boatman with a paddle smiles and hands you a lantern.
“This is Palawan [pah-LAH-wahn],” says Mossy. “And this river goes right through a mountain, underground, for miles and miles, before it reaches the sea.”

The boat glides into the dark. Your lantern lights up the ceiling, high above, as tall as a church. Rock icicles hang down, shining and dripping. Drip. Drip. Tiny birds swoop past in the dark, making little clicking sounds.
“Swiftlets,” whispers Mossy. “They click to find their way, and listen for the echo.”
Mossy tries it. “Click,” he says, in his big moose voice. “CLICK.” The echo comes back: CLICK, CLICK, click. A swiftlet swoops past his nose, as if to say, not bad.
You glide back out into the sunshine, blinking. “Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
You land in a quiet green forest, on the island of Bohol. A guide in a wide straw hat puts a finger to his lips. Shhh. He points to a low branch.

Clinging to the branch is the tiniest animal you have ever seen. It is small enough to sit in your hand, with soft brown fur, a long skinny tail and two enormous round golden eyes, like two full moons.
“A tarsier [TAR-see-er],” whispers Mossy. “Each of its eyes is as big as its whole brain. Its eyes can’t roll around like yours, so it turns its whole head instead.”
Very slowly, the tarsier turns its head, around, and around, until it is looking right behind itself. Then it turns back and blinks at you.
Mossy tries to turn his head all the way around too. He gets about halfway. Then he wobbles, and sits down with a soft thump in the leaves. “Dizzy,” he whispers.
You press your hands over your mouth to keep your giggle quiet. Tarsiers like it very, very quiet. So you tiptoe away, and the tiny tarsier closes its moon eyes for its daytime nap.

As the sun sets, you come to a little house on stilts, beside the water, built from bamboo with a roof of palm leaves. It is called a bahay kubo. A cool breeze blows up through the bamboo floor. You climb into a bed woven from rattan and snuggle under a soft cotton sheet.

Outside, in the mangrove trees, something begins to glow. One tiny light. Then ten. Then thousands. Fireflies, blinking on and off together, until the trees look like they are covered in twinkling holiday lights.

The water laps softly under the house. Lap. Lap. Up in the mountains, the rice terraces are drinking the evening rain. In the cave, the swiftlets have tucked into their nests. And in the forest, the tarsier is just waking up, for its night of hopping and hunting bugs under the moon.

With every blink of the fireflies, Mossy gets a little smaller, until he is pillow-sized again. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Magandang gabi [mah-gahn-DAHNG gah-BEE]. It means good evening. Word for word, it says beautiful night.”
“Magandang gabi,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and watch the fireflies in the mangrove trees. On. Off. On. Off. Let your breathing go slow, in time with their twinkling lights.
nights.alt: Mossy under a plaid blanket. Out the window, green rice terraces step down a misty mountainside. An open journal shows a map of the Philippines.

nights.title: The Land of the Long White Cloud and the Moose Mystery
nights.pronunciations: Aotearoa [ah-oh-teh-ah-ROH-ah], the Māori name for New Zealand; Māori [MAO-ree], the first people of New Zealand; waka [WAH-kah], a voyaging canoe; Pō mārie [paw MAH-ree-eh], good night, in Māori.
nights.anchor: About 1300 AD (Polynesian voyagers arrive in New Zealand by waka, finding their way by the stars, the waves and the birds).
facts: The Long White Cloud:
One Māori name for New Zealand is Aotearoa, often translated as the Land of the Long White Cloud. Ocean voyagers could spot land by the clouds that gathered above it.
A Land of Birds:
Before people arrived, New Zealand had no land mammals except a few kinds of bats. Birds lived everywhere, and some, like the kiwi, stopped flying.
The Kiwi:
The kiwi is round, fluffy and cannot fly. Its nostrils are at the very tip of its long beak, so it can sniff out worms in the ground.
Bubbling Ground:
In Rotorua, heat from deep underground makes steaming lakes, bubbling mud pools and the Pōhutu geyser, which can shoot water about 100 feet high.
The Moose Mystery:
In 1910, ten moose from Canada were set free in the Fiordland forests. None have been seen for a very long time, but a few people are still searching for signs of them.
story: Mossy is holding an old, crinkly photograph very close to his goggles. It shows a thick green forest, and in the corner, something big and brown and blurry.
“Is that a moose?” you ask.
“That,” says Mossy, “is a mystery. And tonight we’re going to look for it. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You are flying high over the ocean. Deep blue water stretches in every direction. There is no land anywhere. Just waves, and sky, and seabirds gliding beside you.

“Long ago,” says Mossy, “people sailed across this ocean in great canoes called waka [WAH-kah]. They had no maps. No compass. Instead, they read the stars at night, the shape of the waves, and the birds flying home in the evening. And when they saw a long white cloud resting on the sea, they knew there was land underneath.”
You look ahead. Far away, a long white cloud is lying across the water, like a soft pillow. And under it, green mountains rise from the sea.
“Aotearoa [ah-oh-teh-ah-ROH-ah],” says Mossy softly. “The Land of the Long White Cloud. Welcome to New Zealand.”
You land beside a lake that is steaming, even though the air is cool. The ground smells a little like eggs. And nearby, a pool of gray mud is bubbling. Bloop. Blorp. Bloop-bloop.
“Deep underground, it’s very hot,” says Mossy. “So the water steams and the mud bubbles, like porridge on the stove.”
He leans over to look. BLORP! A big bubble pops, and a splash of warm gray mud lands right on the end of his nose.
Mossy crosses his eyes to look at it. “Well,” he says. “Now I have a mud moustache.”
You burst out laughing. And behind you, WHOOSH, a geyser shoots a tall fountain of hot water into the sky, as if it’s laughing too.
“Goggles on,” says Mossy, wiping his nose on a fern. WHOOSH!
Now you land in a deep, dark forest, far in the south. Tall mountains rise above you, and misty waterfalls tumble down their sides. Everything is green and dripping with moss.

“This is Fiordland,” whispers Mossy. “More than a hundred years ago, ten moose from Canada were brought here and set free. Moose, all the way down here! And then they vanished into the forest. Nobody has seen one for a very, very long time. But some people are still looking.” He pushes up his goggles. “And tonight, so are we.”
You walk quietly along a mossy path. It is getting dark. Mossy snaps a big silver fern off a low branch and lays it on the ground, silver side up. It shines in the moonlight like a little lamp.
“Māori [MAO-ree] travelers used silver ferns to mark their path at night,” he whispers. “So we can always find our way back.”
Along a creek bank, tiny blue lights begin to glow, hundreds of them, like stars that fell into the forest. “Glowworms,” breathes Mossy.
Then something rustles in the leaves. Crunch. Crunch.
Mossy freezes. His ears stand straight up. “Cousin?” he whispers.

Out of the ferns steps... a bird. A round, fluffy, brown bird, about the size of a football, with no wings you can see and a very long beak. It sniffs the ground with the tip of its beak. Sniff, sniff.
“A kiwi,” whispers Mossy, a little bit disappointed and a lot delighted. “Its nose is at the very end of its beak, so it can sniff for worms.”
The kiwi looks up at Mossy. Mossy looks down at the kiwi. It gives a small, sharp whistle. Then it waddles off into the dark.

You search a little longer. You find ferns and moss and a sleepy owl. You don’t find a moose. But when you turn back, you see a big, round dent in the soft mud by the creek. It might be a hoofprint. Or it might just be a hole.
Mossy looks at it for a long time. Then he smiles. “A mystery is a good thing to keep,” he says.
You follow your trail of silver ferns to a little wooden lodge, where a fire crackles in a stone fireplace. You climb into bed under a blanket made of soft merino wool, as light and warm as a cloud.

Through the window, the southern stars are shining. There is the Southern Cross, four bright stars like a kite, the same stars the waka sailors followed. The kiwi is snuffling for worms in the moonlight. The glowworms glitter by the creek. And somewhere in the deep green forest, maybe, just maybe, a moose is fast asleep.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size and snuggles into the soft merino blanket. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Pō mārie [paw MAH-ree-eh].”
“Pō mārie,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and follow your trail of silver ferns through the dark green forest, one shining fern at a time. Somewhere deep in the moss, maybe, just maybe, a moose is dreaming too.
nights.alt: Mossy under a white blanket printed with ferns. Out the window, snowy mountains and the four stars of the Southern Cross shine over a lake. An open journal shows a map of New Zealand.

nights.title: The Dancing Birds and the River of Many Languages
nights.pronunciations: Sepik [SEE-pik], the great winding river; bilum [BEE-loom], a string bag woven by hand; Tok Pisin [tok PIH-sin], a language many people share; Gut nait [goot NITE], good night, in Tok Pisin.
nights.anchor: About 7,000 years ago or more (farmers at Kuk Swamp dig ditches and grow bananas and taro, some of the earliest farming anywhere in the world).
facts: Hundreds of Languages:
More than 800 languages are spoken in Papua New Guinea, more than in any other country. Many people also share Tok Pisin, English or Hiri Motu.
Birds of Paradise:
Most of the world’s birds-of-paradise live on the island of New Guinea. The males have amazing feathers and do dances to show them off.
A Bird on the Flag:
The Raggiana bird-of-paradise, with its long red and orange plumes, is the national bird. A golden outline of the Raggiana appears on the country’s flag.
The Bilum:
A bilum is a stretchy string bag woven by hand. People use them to carry food, belongings, and even sleeping babies.
The Sepik River:
The long, winding Sepik River is famous for its villages of skilled wood carvers and canoes carved from single tree trunks.
story: Mossy is standing on your bed, holding your blanket out wide behind him like a cape. He hops to the left. He hops to the right. He wiggles his antlers.
“What are you doing?” you ask.
“Dancing,” says Mossy, a little out of breath. “Tonight we’re meeting the best dancers in the whole world. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land in a long wooden canoe, gliding along a wide brown river. Thick green jungle grows right down to the water. The air is warm and wet, and full of bird calls. Hoo-hoo. Wok-wok. Tweedle-eee.
At the front of the canoe, the wood is carved into the face of a smiling crocodile.
“The Sepik [SEE-pik] River, in Papua New Guinea,” says Mossy, trailing one hoof in the warm water. “People here are wonderful wood carvers. This whole canoe was made from one single tree trunk.”

The canoe stops at a village of houses on tall stilts. A woman walks down to the river carrying a colorful string bag on her head. The bag hangs down her back, and inside it, snuggled like a caterpillar in a cocoon, is a sleeping baby.

“A bilum [BEE-loom],” whispers Mossy. “It’s a bag woven by hand from string. People carry everything in them. Sweet potatoes. Books. And babies!” The baby yawns a tiny yawn and keeps sleeping, rocking gently as her mother walks.
The woman smiles and says something you don’t understand. Then a man says something else, which sounds completely different. Then a boy says, “Moning!”

“Papua New Guinea has more than eight hundred languages,” says Mossy. “More than any other country on Earth. Tall mountains and deep forests kept villages apart for a very long time, so each one grew its own way of talking. But lots of people also speak Tok Pisin [tok PIH-sin] so they can understand each other.”
“Moning!” you say to the boy. He laughs and waves.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

Now you land high in the misty mountains, in a cool, green forest dripping with moss and orchids. A guide with a feather in his hat leads you to a hiding place behind some big leaves. “Shhh,” he whispers. “Watch.”

A bird lands on a branch. It is small and black. Then, suddenly, it spreads out its feathers into a huge black cape, shaped like a big oval. Across the middle is a bright blue stripe, like a smile. The bird hops. It bounces. It clicks. It swishes from side to side, with its big blue smile going back and forth.
“A superb bird-of-paradise,” breathes Mossy. “He’s dancing to impress a lady bird.”
Then you hear a loud call from high in the trees. Wau! Wau! Another bird is bowing and shaking long, feathery plumes of red and orange that spill down like a waterfall of fire.
“And that is the Raggiana bird-of-paradise,” whispers the guide proudly. “The bird of our country.”
Mossy can’t help himself. He stands up. He spreads out his scarf like a cape. He hops to the left. He hops to the right. He wiggles his antlers and swishes his tail.
The superb bird-of-paradise stops dancing. It stares at him. The Raggiana stops calling. It stares too. The whole forest is quiet.
Then the little bird puffs up its cape and dances even harder, as if to say, you’ll have to do better than that.
You hide your face in the leaves to keep your giggles in. The guide laughs too.

The sun slips down behind the mountains, and the forest turns soft and blue. The birds fold away their beautiful feathers and tuck their heads down to sleep. You come to a little house on stilts with a roof of palm leaves, and climb into a bamboo bed under a soft cotton quilt, with a white net hanging all around like a cozy tent.

Outside, frogs are singing in the dark. Creek-creek. Creek-creek. The rain has stopped, and the forest smells of wet leaves and flowers. Down on the river, the crocodile canoe bobs quietly at the dock. The baby is asleep in her bilum. And the birds of paradise are resting high in the trees, their fancy feathers folded away until morning.
Mossy folds his scarf away, the way the birds folded their feathers, and shrinks back to pillow size. “Whisper it with me,” he murmurs. “Gut nait [goot NITE].”
“Gut nait,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and curl up like the baby in her bilum, snug as a caterpillar in a cocoon. Feel yourself rocking, gently, gently, as the frogs sing creek-creek in the dark.
nights.alt: Mossy under a woven brown blanket. Out the window, a wide river winds through misty green jungle hills. A lantern glows beside the Bedtime Passport and an open journal.
