weeks.region: The High Andes & the Amazon Basin

nights.title: The City in the Clouds and the Floating Islands
nights.pronunciations: Machu Picchu [MAH-choo PEEK-choo], the stone city in the mountains; Titicaca [tee-tee-KAH-kah], the high lake; totora [toh-TOH-rah], the reeds used to build floating islands; Allin tuta [AH-yeen TOO-tah], good night, in Quechua.
nights.anchor: About 1450 (the Inca build Machu Picchu high in the Andes Mountains).
facts: Stones That Fit Like a Puzzle:
At Machu Picchu, Inca builders shaped granite blocks to fit so tightly that no cement was needed, and in many walls you can’t slip a sheet of paper between the stones.
Floating Islands:
On Lake Titicaca, the Uros people build islands, houses and boats from bundles of totora reeds. Walking on an island feels soft and springy.
A Very High Lake:
Lake Titicaca sits about 12,500 feet up in the mountains. It is often called the highest lake in the world that big boats can travel on.
The Home of Potatoes:
Potatoes were first grown in the Andes thousands of years ago. Peru has thousands of kinds, in colors like purple, red and yellow.
Llamas and Alpacas:
Llamas can carry packs on mountain trails, and alpacas grow very soft wool. Alpacas often talk to each other with a gentle humming sound.
story: Mossy is building a wall with your wooden blocks. But he isn’t using any glue. He turns each block around and around, until it fits snugly against the others. Click.
“There,” he says. “Not one gap. Tonight we’re visiting people who built a whole city this way, on top of a mountain. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land on a high mountain ridge, wrapped in cool white cloud. You can’t see anything but mist. Then, slowly, the cloud begins to lift, like a curtain opening.
And there, on a green mountaintop, between two tall pointy peaks, is a city made of stone.
“Welcome to Machu Picchu [MAH-choo PEEK-choo], in Peru,” whispers Mossy, pushing up his goggles. “The Inca people built it more than five hundred years ago. Look at the walls.”
You walk up to a wall made of big gray stones. Some are as big as a car. And they fit together perfectly, with curvy edges that match like puzzle pieces.
“No cement,” says Mossy. “No glue. They just shaped the stones so carefully that they fit. Try to slip a leaf in between them.”
You try. The leaf won’t go in. Not even a tiny bit.
“And when the ground shakes in an earthquake,” says Mossy, “the stones can jiggle a little, and then settle right back into place.”
Something soft bumps your elbow. You turn around. A fluffy animal with a long neck, big dark eyes and a fringe of wool on its forehead is looking at you. Then it hums. Mmmmm.
“An alpaca,” says Mossy. “Alpacas hum to talk to each other.”
Mossy hums back, in his deep, rumbly moose voice. MMMMMMM.

The alpaca stops. Two more alpacas come over. They all stare at Mossy. Then all three of them hum at once. Mmmm-mmmm-mmmm. Mossy hums with them, and soon you are all standing in the clouds in a little humming choir.
You sit down on the grass, giggling.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
Now you land somewhere soft. Very soft. Your feet sink a little with every step. Squish. Squish.
You are standing on an island made of dry, golden reeds, floating on a huge blue lake. Snowy mountains sparkle far away.

“This is Lake Titicaca [tee-tee-KAH-kah],” says Mossy. “It is so high up in the mountains that it’s closer to the clouds than most lakes in the world. And these islands float! The Uros people make them from reeds called totora [toh-TOH-rah]. They tie big bundles together, and pile on more and more, until they have an island big enough for houses.”
A girl in a bright pink skirt and a little round hat takes your hand. She shows you how to bounce on the reeds. Boing. Boing. It feels like jumping on a giant bed.
Mossy bounces too. Boing. BOING. On his third bounce, he goes so high that he lands on his bottom, FLUMP, and the whole island wobbles like jelly.
“Hmm,” says Mossy. “Moose are a bit heavy for bouncing.” The girl laughs and helps you pull him up. Heave-ho!

Then the girl’s father paddles over in a boat made of reeds, too, with a curly puma head at the front. He gives you a ride across the water. The lake is so still that the mountains look like they are upside down in it.
On the shore, a farmer is sorting potatoes into baskets. But they aren’t just brown. Some are purple. Some are red. Some are bright yellow, and some are long and bumpy like little fingers.
“Potatoes come from here,” says Mossy. “People in these mountains grew them first, thousands of years ago. Now Peru has thousands of kinds.”

The sun sets behind the mountains, and the sky turns gold, then rose, then deep blue. It gets chilly. You walk to a little stone house with a roof made of straw. Inside, a fire crackles. You climb into a wooden bed piled with thick blankets made of soft alpaca wool, warm as a hug.

Through the window, the stars come out, bright and close, because you are so high up. The reed islands rock gently on the dark lake. The alpacas have folded their legs and are resting close together on the hillside, humming softly now and then. And far away, on its mountaintop, the stone city of Machu Picchu is tucked under a blanket of cloud.
Mossy hums one last, soft alpaca hum as he shrinks back to pillow size. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Allin tuta [AH-yeen TOO-tah]. It means good night, in Quechua, the language of the mountains.”
“Allin tuta,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and float on your soft reed island, rocking gently on the dark, still lake. Up on the hillside, the alpacas are humming. Mmmmm. Hum along with them, very quietly, inside your head.
nights.alt: Mossy under a bright woven Andean blanket. Out the window, the stone city of Machu Picchu sits on a misty green mountaintop. An open journal shows a map of Peru and a llama.

nights.title: The River as Wide as the Sea
nights.pronunciations: Amazonas [ah-mah-ZOH-nahs], the Amazon, in Portuguese; boto [BOH-toh], the pink river dolphin; vitória-régia [vee-TOR-yah HEH-zhee-ah], the giant water lily; Boa noite [BOH-ah NOY-chee], good night, in Portuguese.
nights.anchor: About 10 million years ago (the Amazon River begins flowing east across South America into the Atlantic Ocean).
facts: The Mightiest River:
The Amazon carries more water than any other river on Earth, more than the next several biggest rivers put together. In some places you can’t see the other side.
Pink River Dolphins:
Botos are dolphins that live in rivers. Many turn pink as they grow up, and they can bend their necks to wiggle between flooded trees.
Giant Water Lilies:
The leaves of the Amazon giant water lily can grow more than 8 feet across, with turned-up edges like a baking pan.
A Forest Full of Life:
The Amazon rainforest is home to about one in every ten kinds of animals and plants known on Earth.
Sleepy Sloths:
Sloths live high in the trees and move very slowly. They sleep a lot, and they are surprisingly good swimmers.
story: Mossy is sitting in your bathtub with a toy boat. He is pushing it across the water. “Tooooot,” he says.
“That’s a very small river,” you say.
“Exactly,” says Mossy. “Tonight we’re going to the biggest river in the whole world. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land on the wooden deck of a riverboat, chugging along on wide, brown water. The air is warm and sticky and smells of rain and flowers. You look for the other side of the river. You look and look. It is so far away, it’s just a thin green line.

“The Amazon River, in Brazil,” says Mossy, squinting at the faraway shore. “It carries more water than any other river on Earth. More than the next several biggest rivers put together! When it reaches the ocean, it pushes fresh water far out into the salty sea.”
“It looks like the sea,” you say.
“That’s why people call it the River Sea,” says Mossy.
On both sides, the rainforest rises up like a giant green wall. Monkeys chatter. Parrots squawk. A toucan with a huge, bright orange beak hops along a branch, like it’s wearing a banana on its face.
Then something pops up out of the water right beside the boat. Pfffffff! It blows a little spray of mist into the air.
It’s a dolphin. A pink dolphin!
“A boto [BOH-toh],” says Mossy. “A river dolphin. They turn pinker as they grow up. And look how it bends its neck! It can wiggle between the trees when the forest floods.”
The boto swims alongside you, then dives. Pfffffff. It pops up again, on the other side, and looks right at Mossy.

“Hello,” says Mossy. “I can swim too, you know. Moose are very good swimmers.” The boto bends its neck, flips its tail and swims a fast, twisty circle all the way around him. Swish! “Show-off,” Mossy mutters, smiling.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

Now you land at the edge of a quiet, glassy pond in the forest. Floating on the water are the biggest leaves you have ever seen. They are round and flat, like giant green pizza pans, with little turned-up edges all around. Some of them are wider than your whole bed.
“Giant water lilies,” says Mossy. “Their leaves are strong enough to hold up a frog, a heron, or a whole family of little birds.” He looks at the leaves thoughtfully. “And maybe a moose?”
“I don’t think so,” you say.
Mossy puts one hoof on a lily pad. It holds. He puts on another hoof. It holds. He puts on a third hoof. The lily pad tips, very slowly, and Mossy slides off into the pond with a big, gentle SPLOOSH.
He pops up with a small green frog sitting on top of his helmet. The frog blinks. “Not a moose,” he agrees.
You laugh so hard a family of birds flaps out of the reeds.
Mossy swims back to shore and shakes himself off. Then he points his dripping nose up into a tall tree. “Look up there. Very slowly.”
Hanging from a branch, upside down, is a furry animal with a sleepy smile and long, curved claws. It turns its head toward you. Veeeeery slowly.
“A sloth,” whispers Mossy. “Sloths move so slowly that tiny green plants grow in their fur. They sleep for a lot of the day. And they are really good swimmers too.”
The sloth blinks. Slowly. Mossy blinks back. Slowly. It is a staring contest that nobody wins, because the sloth falls asleep.

As the sun sets, the sky turns orange and pink, and the whole river glows like melted gold. You climb back onto the riverboat. On the top deck, colorful hammocks are strung between the posts, swaying in the breeze.
“On Amazon riverboats,” says Mossy, “people sleep in hammocks.”
You climb into a soft cotton hammock. It wraps around you like a cocoon and rocks you, gently, back and forth, back and forth, as the boat chugs slowly down the river.

The rainforest is full of night sounds. Frogs croak. Crickets chirp. Somewhere far off, a howler monkey calls a low good night. The toucan has tucked its big beak under its wing. The boto is resting in a quiet bend of the river. The giant lily leaves float still and flat on the dark pond. And the sloth is still hanging in its tree, fast asleep, exactly where you left it.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, still smelling a little of pond, and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Boa noite [BOH-ah NOY-chee]. It means good night, in Portuguese.”
“Boa noite,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and feel your hammock rocking, back and forth, back and forth. Now blink as slowly as the sloth. Slower. Slower still. Until you forget to open your eyes at all.
nights.alt: Mossy under a blanket printed with green palm leaves. Out the window, a full moon shines over a wide river winding through the rainforest. An open journal shows a map of Brazil.

nights.title: The Line Around the Middle and the Giant Tortoises
nights.pronunciations: Mitad del Mundo [mee-TAHD del MOON-doh], the Middle of the World; Galápagos [gah-LAH-pah-gohs], the tortoise islands; Chimborazo [cheem-boh-RAH-soh], the tall volcano; Buenas noches [BWAY-nahs NOH-chays], good night, in Spanish.
nights.anchor: 1835 (the young scientist Charles Darwin visits the Galápagos Islands and studies their birds and tortoises).
facts: The Middle of the World:
The equator, the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, runs through Ecuador. That is how the country got its name: Ecuador is Spanish for equator.
Closest to the Stars:
Because the Earth bulges a little around its middle, the top of Mount Chimborazo is the farthest point from the center of the Earth, even farther than the top of Mount Everest.
Giant Tortoises:
Galápagos tortoises can weigh more than 500 pounds and live for more than 100 years.
Swimming Lizards:
Marine iguanas are the only lizards in the world that swim in the ocean to find food. They sneeze out the extra salt from the seawater.
Blue Feet:
Blue-footed boobies are seabirds with bright blue feet. They lift their feet high in a funny dance to show them off.
story: Mossy is holding your globe. He is running his hoof around the middle of it, along a thin line. Around and around.
“This line is called the equator,” he says. “It goes all the way around the middle of the Earth, like a belt. Tonight we’re going to stand right on it. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land in bright sunshine, high in the mountains. In front of you is a tall stone monument with a big globe on top. And on the ground, there is a long painted yellow line.
“The Mitad del Mundo [mee-TAHD del MOON-doh],” says Mossy, tapping the yellow line with his hoof. “That means the Middle of the World. We’re in Ecuador. Ecuador is the Spanish word for equator!”
You put one foot on each side of the line. “Now one foot is in the top half of the world,” says Mossy, “and one foot is in the bottom half.”
Mossy tries it too. He has four legs, so he puts two hooves on each side. Then he looks at the map on the monument. Then he looks at the line. Then he frowns.

“Here’s a funny secret,” he whispers. “When people used satellites to check, they found the real equator is a short walk that way.” He points his antler down the hill. “The painted line is in a slightly wrong place!”
So you walk down the hill, together, counting steps, until Mossy stops and says, “Here. Probably.” And you both stand on the real middle of the world, which has no line at all.

Far away, a giant snowy volcano rises into the sky. “Chimborazo [cheem-boh-RAH-soh],” says Mossy. “The Earth is a little bit fat around the middle, like a moose after dinner. So the top of that mountain sticks out farther into space than anywhere else. It’s the closest place on Earth to the stars.”
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
You fly far out over the ocean and land on a black, rocky island. Waves splash against the shore. The rocks are warm from the sun.
“The Galápagos [gah-LAH-pah-gohs] Islands,” says Mossy. “They are so far away from everywhere that the animals here grew up in their own special ways. And they aren’t afraid of people.”
Something big is walking toward you, very slowly. Step. Pause. Step. It is a tortoise. But not a small one. This tortoise is as big as an armchair, with a huge, domed shell and a long, wrinkly neck.
“A giant tortoise,” whispers Mossy. “It might weigh as much as a piano. And it might be more than a hundred years old.”
The tortoise stretches out its neck and slowly chews a bite of green leaves. Crunch. Crunch.

Mossy lies down so his nose is right in front of the tortoise’s nose. “Hello, Grandpa,” he says. The tortoise looks at him for a long time. Then it breathes out, HUFFFF, a big puff of air right in his face. Mossy’s ears blow back.
“I think that means hello,” he says.
Down by the water, dark lizards are lying in a heap on the warm rocks, like a pile of spiky black socks.

“Marine iguanas,” says Mossy. “The only lizards in the world that swim in the sea. They dive down to eat seaweed.” One iguana lifts its head. It looks at Mossy. And then... ACHOO! It sneezes, and a little spray of salty water lands right on his helmet.
“They sneeze out the salt from the seawater,” says Mossy, wiping his goggles. “I just didn’t expect it to be on me.”
You giggle and almost tumble onto the iguanas.
On the beach, a bird with bright blue feet is lifting one foot. Then the other. Then the first one again, very high, like he is marching in a parade.
“A blue-footed booby,” says Mossy. “He’s showing off his beautiful blue feet.” You lift your feet high too, left, right, left, right. The booby watches you. Then he whistles, as if to say, not bad.

The sun sinks into the Pacific Ocean, red and orange. Bright red crabs scuttle into the cracks in the rocks. You walk to a little wooden cabin beside a quiet beach and climb into a bed with a light cotton quilt. A cool breeze blows in off the sea.

Right above you, the stars come out, sparkling over the middle of the world. The marine iguanas are snuggled together in one big heap to stay warm. The booby has tucked his blue feet under him. And the giant tortoise has pulled his head and legs inside his shell, like a house with the lights turned off.

Mossy tucks in his head and legs, just like the tortoise, and when he pops back out, he is pillow-sized again. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Buenas noches [BWAY-nahs NOH-chays]. It means good night, in Spanish.”
“Buenas noches,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and be the giant tortoise. Slowly, slowly, pull in your head. Pull in your arms. Pull in your legs. Now you are snug inside your shell, like a house with the lights turned off.
nights.alt: Mossy under a striped Andean blanket. Out the window, a snowcapped volcano rises against the night sky. An open journal shows a map of Ecuador.

nights.title: The Giant Mirror of Salt
nights.capital: Sucre [SOO-kray] and La Paz [lah PAHS] (Bolivia has two capitals)
nights.pronunciations: Salar de Uyuni [sah-LAR day oo-YOO-nee], the great salt flat; Laguna Colorada [lah-GOO-nah koh-loh-RAH-dah], the red lake; teleférico [teh-leh-FEH-ree-koh], a cable car; Aski arumakipana [AHS-kee ah-roo-mah-kee-PAH-nah], good night, in Aymara.
nights.anchor: Tens of thousands of years ago (a giant ancient lake dries up in the high Andes and leaves behind the Salar de Uyuni).
facts: The Biggest Salt Flat:
The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world, more than 4,000 square miles of white salt, high in the Andes Mountains.
A Mirror on the Ground:
In the rainy season, a thin layer of water covers the salt, and it reflects the sky so perfectly that the clouds seem to be under your feet.
Cable Car Buses:
In La Paz and El Alto, people ride cable cars across the city, high above the streets. It is one of the highest and longest city cable car networks in the world.
The Red Lake:
Laguna Colorada is colored red by tiny algae, and flocks of pink flamingos feed there.
Many Languages:
Bolivia has more than 30 official languages, including Spanish, Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní.
story: Mossy is licking the salt shaker. Lick. Lick. He looks up, a little embarrassed.

“Moose love salt,” he explains. “Back home, we go looking for salty mud to lick. It’s a moose treat.” He licks again. “And tonight, we’re visiting the biggest pile of salt in the whole world. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land inside a little glass cabin, swinging high in the air on a cable. Below you is a huge city, spilling down the sides of a mountain valley, with snowy peaks all around.

“La Paz, in Bolivia,” says Mossy, swaying gently as the little cabin glides along. “This city is so high up in the mountains that you’re almost in the clouds. And instead of just buses, people ride cable cars to get around!”

The cable car glides smoothly over rooftops and streets. You see a boy on a balcony waving at you. You wave back. You see a grandmother in a round bowler hat and a big, puffy, colorful skirt, hanging out her laundry. She waves too.
Mossy presses his nose against the glass to see better. Squish. When he pulls away, there is a big foggy moose-nose print on the window. You draw a smiley face in it.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

Now you land on something white and flat and crunchy. It goes on and on, as far as you can see, in every direction. Flat. Perfectly flat. And across the whole thing lies a thin layer of clear water, like a giant puddle.
Then you look down, and you gasp.
The sky is under your feet. The fluffy white clouds, the bright blue sky, the snowy mountains, all reflected perfectly in the water. It looks like you are standing in the middle of the sky.

“This is the Salar de Uyuni [sah-LAR day oo-YOO-nee],” says Mossy. “Long, long ago, there was a huge lake up here. It dried up, and all that was left was salt. Now it’s the biggest salt flat in the world. And when it rains, it turns into the biggest mirror in the world.”
You walk across the mirror. Splish. Splash. Your reflection walks upside down underneath you. It feels like flying.
Mossy has gone very quiet. He is staring down at the ground.
“It’s all salt,” he whispers. “All of it.”
He bends down and gives it one lick. Then another. Then he lies down flat on his tummy and licks it with a happy slurp. Slllllurp.
“Mossy!” you laugh.
“A moose treat,” he says dreamily, “as big as the sky.” You laugh so hard you sit down with a splash, right in the middle of a cloud.
“Goggles on,” says Mossy at last, with salt on his whiskers. WHOOSH!
You land beside a lake that is red. Not blue. Red, like strawberry juice, with white edges like frosting. Around it are brown mountains and a bright blue sky.
“Laguna Colorada [lah-GOO-nah koh-loh-RAH-dah],” says Mossy. “The red lake. Tiny, tiny plants called algae live in the water and turn it red.”
And standing in the red water, on long skinny legs, are flamingos. Hundreds of pink flamingos, dipping their curved beaks into the lake, upside down, to eat. Some honk softly. Honk. Honk.
A fuzzy llama with pom-pom tassels in its ears wanders over and sniffs Mossy’s salty whiskers. Then it licks them. Lick.
“Fair enough,” says Mossy. “Everyone likes salt.”
The sun goes down, and the whole sky turns pink and orange, and the flamingos turn pinker than ever. It gets chilly, so you walk to a small hotel at the edge of the salt flat.
And the hotel is made of salt! The walls are salt blocks. The table is salt. Even the bed is built from salt blocks. Mossy looks at the walls, very tempted. You shake your head. He sighs.
You climb into the bed, on a soft mattress, under thick blankets of sheep and llama wool.

Outside, the night is clear and very dark, far from any town. The stars come out. Thousands of them. Millions. And they shine in the sky above and in the water below, until it feels as if you are floating in a big ball of stars. The flamingos are standing on one leg, fast asleep. The llama is curled up with its herd. And the cable cars in the city have stopped, resting on their wires high above the quiet streets.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, licks one last grain of salt off his nose, and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Aski arumakipana [AHS-kee ah-roo-mah-kee-PAH-nah]. It means good night, in Aymara, one of the languages of the mountains.”
“Aski arumakipana,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and float in the big ball of stars, with stars above you and stars below you. You are not falling. You are just floating, soft and light, in the middle of the sky.
nights.alt: Mossy under a striped woven blanket. Out the window, a vast flat salt plain reflects the starry sky. An open journal shows a map of Bolivia.

nights.title: The Driest Desert and the Stone Giants
nights.pronunciations: Atacama [ah-tah-KAH-mah], the driest desert; Rapa Nui [RAH-pah NOO-ee], the island also called Easter Island; moai [MOH-eye], the great stone statues; Que duermas bien [keh DWEHR-mahs bee-EN], sleep well, in Spanish.
nights.anchor: About 1250 to 1500 (the Rapa Nui people carve most of the moai statues from volcanic rock).
facts: A Long, Skinny Country:
Chile is more than 2,600 miles long but, on average, only about 110 miles wide, squeezed between the Andes Mountains and the Pacific Ocean.
The Driest Desert:
The Atacama is the driest desert in the world outside the North and South Poles. Some places there have gone years without rain.
A Window to the Stars:
The Atacama’s dry, clear air makes it one of the best places on Earth to study the stars, so astronomers from many countries have built giant telescopes there.
The Moai:
Nearly 900 giant stone statues called moai stand on Rapa Nui. The Rapa Nui people carved them to honor their ancestors, and old stories say the statues “walked” to their places.
Condors and Guanacos:
In Patagonia, Andean condors soar on wings about 10 feet across, and guanacos, wild cousins of the llama, graze on the grass.
story: Mossy is standing in the corner of your room. Very, very still. He isn’t blinking. He isn’t wiggling. He isn’t even twitching an ear.
“Mossy?” you whisper.
“I’m a statue,” he whispers back, without moving his lips. “Practicing. Tonight we meet the biggest statues in the Pacific Ocean. But first, a desert. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You land on dry, rusty-red ground. There are no trees. No grass. Not even a puddle. Just rocks and sand and wrinkly brown hills, and far away, snowy volcanoes.

“The Atacama [ah-tah-KAH-mah] Desert, in Chile,” says Mossy, shading his eyes from the bright sun. “It is the driest desert in the world, except for the icy places at the very top and bottom of the Earth. Some places here have gone years and years without a single drop of rain.”
Mossy licks his lips. “My nose feels like a cracker,” he says.
On top of a hill, you see a row of huge white dishes, all pointing up at the sky, like giant ears listening to space.
“Telescopes,” says Mossy. “The air here is so dry and clear that it’s one of the best places on Earth to look at the stars. Scientists come from all over the world to study them.”
The sun is shining now. But you can already tell that tonight’s sky is going to be something special.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
You fly west, far out over the Pacific Ocean, for a long, long time. Waves. Waves. More waves. And then, at last, a small green island, all by itself in the middle of the sea.
You land on a grassy hillside. And standing in front of you, in a line, are giant stone people.

They are huge, as tall as two grown-ups standing on each other’s shoulders. They have long faces, big noses and serious eyebrows. They are standing with their backs to the ocean, looking out over the island.

“Moai [MOH-eye],” whispers Mossy. “Welcome to Rapa Nui [RAH-pah NOO-ee], an island that is part of Chile. The Rapa Nui people carved these statues out of volcanic rock, hundreds of years ago, to honor their grandparents and great-grandparents. There are nearly nine hundred of them.”
“How did they move them?” you ask. “They’re so big.”

“An old story says the moai walked,” says Mossy. “And some scientists think that’s almost true! With ropes tied on each side, people could rock a statue gently from side to side, and it would shuffle forward, step by step, as if it were walking.”
You imagine a giant stone statue waddling across the grass. Wobble. Wobble.
Mossy lines up at the end of the row of moai. He stands up very straight. He makes a serious face, with serious eyebrows. He doesn’t move at all.
A little brown bird flies down and lands right on top of his helmet. It looks around. It fluffs its feathers. It settles in.
Mossy doesn’t move. But the bird starts to peck at his antlers. Tap. Tap-tap. Mossy’s ears twitch. His lips wobble. And then... “Hee-hee-HEE! That tickles!”
The bird flies off in a flurry. You laugh and laugh, and roll all the way down the grassy hill.
“Statues,” sniffs Mossy, “are harder than they look.”
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

Now you land in the far south, in a cold, windy land called Patagonia. Three tall, pointy mountains of granite rise into the clouds, and a turquoise lake glitters at their feet. Your cheeks tingle from the wind.

Grazing on the hillside are animals that look a bit like llamas, with soft brown and white fur. “Guanacos,” says Mossy, “wild cousins of the llama.” And high above them, a giant black bird is circling, its wings spread wider than a door is tall.
“An Andean condor,” says Mossy. “One of the biggest flying birds in the world. It hardly flaps at all. It just rides the wind.”
Mossy spreads his scarf out wide and leans into the wind. For a moment, his ears flap and his scarf flutters, and he looks almost like he is flying. Then the wind stops, and he tips over into a bush.
At last you fly back north to the desert, where a little lodge made of thick clay bricks waits for you. You climb into a sturdy wooden bed under a heavy wool blanket.
And then you look out the window.

The sky is full. So many stars that you can’t count them. A soft, glowing river of light, the Milky Way, stretches from one side of the sky to the other. Out in the desert, the big telescope ears are listening. The condor is asleep on its high cliff. And far out in the ocean, the moai stand quietly under the same stars, watching over their island.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Que duermas bien [keh DWEHR-mahs bee-EN]. It means sleep well, in Spanish.”
“Que duermas bien,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and lie as still as a stone moai. Very still. Very heavy. Very calm. Above you, the Milky Way flows across the sky like a soft river of light.
nights.alt: Mossy under a tan blanket. Out the window, jagged granite towers rise above the hills of Patagonia. An open journal shows a map of Chile.

nights.title: The Tallest Palms and the Rainbow River
nights.pronunciations: Cocora [koh-KOH-rah], the valley of wax palms; Caño Cristales [KAH-nyoh krees-TAH-lays], the rainbow river; Muisca [MWEES-kah], the people of the golden raft legend; Dulces sueños [DOOL-says SWAY-nyohs], sweet dreams, in Spanish.
nights.anchor: Many hundreds of years ago (Muisca goldsmiths make a tiny golden raft, now kept at the Gold Museum in Bogotá).
facts: The Tallest Palms:
In the Cocora Valley, Quindío wax palms can grow about 200 feet tall. They are the tallest palm trees in the world and Colombia’s national tree.
More Birds Than Anywhere:
Colombia has more kinds of birds than any other country, more than 1,900, including about 165 kinds of hummingbirds.
The Liquid Rainbow:
For part of each year, a water plant in the river Caño Cristales turns bright red and pink, making the water look striped with color.
The Golden Raft:
An old Muisca story tells of a new leader covered in gold dust who floated on a raft onto Lake Guatavita. A tiny golden raft showing this scene is in Bogotá’s Gold Museum.
Coffee Mountains:
Colombian coffee grows on steep mountain slopes, where farmers pick the red coffee cherries by hand.
story: Mossy is standing on tiptoe against your door frame, stretching his neck as high as it will go, with a pencil on his head. He makes a little mark. Then he steps back and looks at it.

“When I grow big for our trips, I’m very tall,” he says, proudly. “Taller than a pony. Taller than the door. Taller than almost everything.” He pauses. “Tonight we’re going to find out if I’m taller than a tree. Goggles on!”

WHOOOOSH! You land in a green valley, early in the morning. Mist floats low over the grass. Cows are munching quietly. And rising up out of the mist are trees. The tallest, skinniest trees you have ever seen.
They go up, and up, and up, with pale gray trunks as smooth as candles, until at the very top, far above the mist, they burst into little green pom-poms of leaves.
“The Cocora [koh-KOH-rah] Valley, in Colombia,” says Mossy, in a hushed voice. “These are wax palms. The tallest palm trees in the world. Some are taller than a twenty-story building.”
Mossy walks up to one. He stands right next to it. He tips his head back, and back, and back, until his helmet slides off.
“Oh,” he says in a small voice. “I am not taller than this tree.”
Then he smiles a big, happy smile. “You know what? I love feeling small. On our trips, it hardly ever happens to me.”
High up in the pom-pom leaves, yellow-eared parrots are chattering. And zipping around the valley, buzzing like tiny helicopters, are hummingbirds, green and blue and shining like jewels.
“Colombia has more kinds of birds than any other country in the world,” says Mossy. “Almost two thousand kinds!”

A hummingbird zooms up to Mossy’s face and hovers right in front of his nose. Bzzzzz. It looks at his left eye. It looks at his right eye. Then it zips up and pokes its long beak into a little pink flower that is caught in his antlers. Sip, sip.
Mossy goes cross-eyed trying to watch it. “I’m a flower pot,” he whispers happily.
You lean on the palm tree, giggling.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
Now you land beside a river. But it isn’t blue. It isn’t brown. It is red! And pink, and yellow, and green, and blue, all in stripes, flowing over smooth gray rocks.

“Caño Cristales [KAH-nyoh krees-TAH-lays],” says Mossy. “People call it the River of Five Colors, or the Liquid Rainbow. For part of every year, a special little plant that grows on the rocks under the water turns bright red and pink. With the yellow sand, the green moss and the blue sky, the whole river looks like a rainbow.”
You dip your toes in. The water is cool and clear. Mossy wades in too, and stands very still, looking down at the red plants waving around his hooves.
“I think my legs look very nice in red,” he says.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
You land beside a round, quiet lake high in the mountains, surrounded by green hills like the edge of a bowl.

“This is Lake Guatavita,” says Mossy softly. “The Muisca [MWEES-kah] people lived here long ago. They told a story about it. When they had a new leader, he was covered all over in shiny gold dust, until he sparkled like the sun. Then he floated out onto the lake on a raft, with music and singing all around, to give thanks.”
“A golden person,” you whisper.
“People called him El Dorado,” says Mossy. “The Golden One. And in a museum in the city, there is a tiny raft made of gold, showing that very scene. It is small enough to fit in your hands.”

As the sun sets, you walk to a farmhouse on a mountainside, painted bright yellow and blue, with a wide porch and hammocks swaying in the breeze. All around it, coffee bushes grow on the steep slopes, dotted with little red berries.
Inside, there is a wooden bed with fresh white sheets and a warm, fuzzy blanket. A cup of warm sweet drink with a cinnamon stick waits on the table. You take a sip and snuggle in.

Outside, the mist is drifting down the mountain, wrapping around the wax palms until only their pom-pom tops poke out. The hummingbirds have tucked themselves into their tiny nests. The rainbow river keeps flowing, quietly, in the dark. And the lake is still and smooth, reflecting one golden star.

Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, pulls the little pink flower out of his antlers, and pulls his goggles down. “Whisper it with me,” he says. “Dulces sueños [DOOL-says SWAY-nyohs]. It means sweet dreams, in Spanish.”
“Dulces sueños,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and dip your toes in the rainbow river. Let the colors flow past, one at a time. Red. Pink. Yellow. Green. Blue. Now let them all fade, softly, into the dark.
nights.alt: Mossy under a colorful patchwork blanket. Out the window, very tall, thin palm trees rise from a misty green valley. An open journal shows a map of Colombia.

nights.title: The Thundering Waterfalls and the Blue Ice Wall
nights.pronunciations: Iguazú [ee-gwah-SOO], the great waterfalls; gaucho [GOW-choh], a cowboy of the grasslands; Perito Moreno [peh-REE-toh moh-REH-noh], the giant glacier; Que descanses [keh dehs-KAHN-says], rest well, in Spanish.
nights.anchor: 1934 (Argentina creates Iguazú National Park to protect the waterfalls and the rainforest around them).
facts: Big Water:
Iguazú Falls, on the border of Argentina and Brazil, is made of about 275 waterfalls. Its name comes from Guaraní words meaning “big water.”
Birds Behind the Falls:
Great dusky swifts build their nests on the wet rocks behind the falling water and fly right through the spray.
The Gauchos:
On the wide grasslands called the pampas, gauchos are skilled horse riders who herd cattle and wear warm woven ponchos.
A Wall of Blue Ice:
The Perito Moreno Glacier in Patagonia ends in a wall of ice about 240 feet high above a lake. Huge chunks break off and splash into the water.
The Tallest Mountain:
Mount Aconcagua in Argentina is about 22,838 feet tall, the highest mountain outside Asia.
story: Mossy is standing by the window with a spray bottle. Psst. Psst. He sprays a little mist into the sunshine, and a tiny rainbow appears.
“Ooh,” he says. “Tonight we’re visiting a place that makes rainbows all day long. Goggles on!”
WHOOOOSH! You hear it before you see it. A deep, rumbling roar, like a thousand bathtubs pouring out at once. ROOOAAARRR.

You land on a long walkway, high above a jungle. And in front of you, water is pouring over cliffs. Not one waterfall. Dozens of them! Hundreds! Crashing down in white curtains, one after another, all the way around a giant curve.
“Iguazú [ee-gwah-SOO] Falls, in Argentina!” shouts Mossy over the roar. “Iguazú means big water. There are about two hundred seventy-five waterfalls here!”

Cool mist floats up and sprinkles your face. And everywhere in the mist, there are rainbows. Rainbows over the water. Rainbows over the trees. Even a small rainbow sitting right on top of Mossy’s antlers.
Little dark birds are zooming in and out of the falling water. “Swifts!” says Mossy. “They build their nests on the wet rocks right behind the waterfalls. They fly straight through!”
Then something tugs at Mossy’s scarf. A furry animal with a long, striped tail and a long, wiggly nose is standing on its back legs, sniffing the end of it.
“A coati,” says Mossy. “They’re very curious. And very sneaky. I don’t have any snacks, little one.”
The coati pokes its nose into his scarf anyway. Then it finds a few grains of salt still stuck on his whiskers from the salt flat, and gives them a lick. Lick, lick.
“Everyone,” sighs Mossy, “loves my whiskers.” You laugh, and the mist gets in your mouth.
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!
Now you land on a wide, flat, grassy plain, stretching out forever under a huge blue sky. The grass ripples in the wind, like the sea.
“The pampas,” says Mossy. “Some of the best grassland in the world.”
Galloping toward you is a man on a brown horse, wearing a wide flat hat and a striped woven poncho. He pulls up and tips his hat. “Buenas tardes,” he says. That means good afternoon.
“A gaucho [GOW-choh],” whispers Mossy. “Gauchos are wonderful horse riders.”
The gaucho lifts you up onto a gentle gray horse. Clip-clop, clip-clop, you ride slowly across the grass. Then a little faster. Clippity-clop, clippity-clop.

Mossy trots along beside you. Then he canters. Then he gallops, his ears flapping, his scarf streaming out behind him. The horses look at him, very surprised. The gaucho laughs so hard he almost loses his hat.
“Moose,” puffs Mossy, “can run faster than you think!”
“Goggles on!” WHOOSH!

You land in the far south, where the air is cold and crisp. You are standing on a wooden path beside a lake of milky blue water. And across the lake is a wall. A wall of ice. Bright blue and white, taller than the tallest building in most towns, and stretching as far as you can see.
“The Perito Moreno [peh-REE-toh moh-REH-noh] Glacier,” whispers Mossy, his eyes shining. “A glacier is a river made of ice. It creeps very, very slowly down from the snowy mountains.”

Then you hear a loud CRACK. A huge chunk of ice, as big as a house, breaks off the wall and falls into the lake. KER-SPLOOOSH! A wave rolls across the water, and the chunk bobs back up, a floating blue ice island.
“Snow and ice,” sighs Mossy happily. “What a way to end the day.”
The sun sets, and the ice turns pink. You walk to a ranch house made of wood and stone, where a fire is glowing in the fireplace. You climb into a big bed under thick, warm wool blankets.

Outside, the wind whispers over the pampas. The horses are resting in the stable. The coati is curled up with its tail over its nose. The swifts are tucked into their nests behind the falls, and far away the waterfalls are still roaring, softly now, like a lullaby. And the ice wall glows quietly under the southern stars.
Mossy shrinks back to pillow size, and the faraway roar of the waterfalls nearly rocks him to sleep. “Whisper it with me,” he murmurs. “Que descanses [keh dehs-KAHN-says]. It means rest well.”
“Que descanses,” you whisper.
nights.dream_seed: Close your eyes and listen to the faraway waterfalls, roaring softly now, like a lullaby. Shhhhhhh. Let the sound wash over you, long and slow, until it is the only thing you hear.
nights.alt: Mossy under a cream blanket with a woven border. Out the window, wide waterfalls pour down cliffs under a crescent moon. An open journal shows a map of Argentina.
